DATA.name: Żerań (OP-Żerań, Z1)
DATA.summary: The hub of the survivor community, on the Vistula at the north of the corridor.
DATA.entry: The hub. Power, radio and water access are routed from here. Class D ground. Grid reference 52.2926 N, 20.9964 E. A radio built from boards, scavenged parts and hand-wound coils stands here, with cable run up the stairwell toward the chimney, and it is among the first things Diana saw there. Janek Dąbrowski sat beside Goya Liszka on the dock at Żerań, early in Goya's time in the zone, and listened to him curse for ten minutes. The abandoned houseboat on which Diana Antonoff lived is moored at Żerań, at the northern edge of the wetlands. The staff gauge on the Żerań dock is read daily at 07:00. The canal is open in summer, with lily pads, reed and a beaver, and frozen at the margins in winter, with ice 11 centimetres thick by 9 December 2034. Diana counted dragonflies of four species at the dock on thirty-one mornings. The Russian post RM, at Tarchomin, lies about three kilometres from the dock and presses directly on the hub. The Dendron was measured in the cooling channel, where a mature mass lowered the water by 11 centimetres in nine days, and it does not grow on the bricks of the power station. The hub was destroyed in the third flood. The lights failed at 02:05 on 1 January 2035, the last in the corridor to do so, and radio contact ended at 03:05 in the middle of a sentence. The occupier watched from the Citadel, with a searchlight, for two and a half hours. The red and white chimney was not brought down. The number of persons at Żerań that night is not recorded.
DATA.appears: Prologue: The Barn. Diary 001: The Arrival. Chapter 1: The Blasphemer (Goya's recording, made at Żerań). Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), the register, the gauge and the canal. Chapter 5: The Pilgrim (the dock, 19 August 2034). Interlude: The Second Flood (the houseboat, 28 August 2034). Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), the Tarchomin post. Chapter 9: The Dendron (Protocol 003), the cooling channel and the power station. Chapter 11: The Orphan (canal ice, 30 November 2034). Chapter 12: The Codex (Protocol 004), the dragonflies at the dock. Chapter 15: The Aftermath (Protocol 005), the destruction of the hub. Chapter 16: The Protocols (the houseboat diaries of December 2034, and the letter).
DATA.reliability: C. More than twelve independent manuscript passages. Function, class and grid reference are from the register in Chapter 3. The destruction on 1 January 2035 is timed in Protocol 005, which its compiler built from nine sources, none of them present at Żerań. The number of persons at Żerań is not recorded.

facts.function: The hub. Power, radio and water access
facts.water_condition: Class D, dry but cut off. The canal is open in summer and frozen in winter, with ice 11 cm thick by 9 December 2034. The dock gauge is read daily at 07:00.
facts.events: Diana arrives, 1 June 2034. Goya's recording is made here. The hub is destroyed in the third flood, 1 January 2035: lights out at 02:05, radio contact ends at 03:05.

DATA.name: Zoo (OP-Zoo, Z2)
DATA.summary: A community gathering place with large grounds and good cover.
DATA.entry: Community gathering. Large grounds, good cover. Class D ground. Grid reference 52.2573 N, 21.0255 E. About two hundred and ten people live in the Zoo, in enclosures that have been made into houses. The lion house is the largest. It has a barred front, which serves as the wall of a stove, and a long hall where the cages were. At about six each evening the people come in from the cold and sit on the floor. The keeper's house is also used. The Dendron reached the lower Zoo in the second flood. A woman at the Zoo leaves a saucer of milk at the foot of the largest mass each morning at seven. The woman at the Zoo is named in Protocol 003 as Mrs Kaczmarek, who believes the Dendron was sent to teach patience. She has been at stage 1 for three months. On 17 November 2034 Diana counted about sixty in the lion house, nineteen of them children, when Tanja Dopolewka played the violin from an upturned feed bin with her back to the old viewing window. Three of Catalina's stage 2 patients wept. The violin carries across the water to the Docks, about two kilometres, when the air is still. Statements from the western powers are read aloud at the Zoo in the evenings. The keeper's house stands at the south end, inside the old reptile garden. It is a small brick house with a pitched roof and a tin chimney, and it belongs to Pan and Pani Wróbel, who have taken in two children, Anna and Nikita. Visitors knock twice and wait, because Nikita is frightened of a single knock.
DATA.appears: Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), the register. Chapter 4: The Engineer (the violin heard from the Docks). Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002). Chapter 7: The Musician (diary of 17 November 2034, and Tanja's recording). Chapter 8: The Medic (the antibiotic course taken to the Zoo). Chapter 9: The Dendron (Protocol 003). Chapter 10: The Listener (Diana's note on Magda). Chapter 13: The Youngest (diary of 26 October 2034 at the keeper's house, and Alisia's recording). Chapter 14: The Mouse (diary of 4 November 2034 at the keeper's house). Chapter 16: The Protocols.
DATA.reliability: C. More than ten independent manuscript passages. Function, class and grid reference are from the register. The count of two hundred and ten is Diana's, given in her diary of 17 November 2034 as the last count, one source, E. Mrs Kaczmarek is named once, in Protocol 003.

facts.function: Community gathering. Large grounds, good cover
facts.water_condition: Class D, dry but cut off. The Dendron reached the lower Zoo in the second flood.
facts.events: The theft at the keeper's house, 26 October 2034. Tanja plays in the lion house, 17 November 2034.

DATA.name: Brodno (OP-Brodno, SZ)
DATA.summary: The old hospital, which the survivors use as their medical post.
DATA.entry: Szpital (Brodno). Medical. Defensible. Multiple buildings. Class D ground. Grid reference 52.2984 N, 21.1071 E. Catalina Chmielewska treats patients with documented exposure here, and she allowed a visitor to sit in the ward at a distance of two metres. A chapel stands on the grounds. Alex's note in Chapter 8: The Medic puts Diana's meeting with Catalina here in the second week of October 2034, and her diary of 11 October 2034 is set in the ward. Catalina's data record 3 of 81 persons exposed at stage 3 or beyond who did not become compliant. All three, on the first day of exposure, were doing something for someone else. Diana's last notes place the three at Brodno. The hospital stands on a low rise and has kept its feet dry. It is a long building in grey brick with four wings and a chapel. The ground floor and the first floor are wards, and every room that is not a ward is a store. Water is carried from a cistern in the yard. In the dispensary a ledger records the stock of each drug and, beside it, the number of people who will not receive it. Pawel keeps the stores. The Brigade has held a hearing in the chapel, with thirty people on the pews. A scientist who had worked eleven years in the laboratory sat on the chapel step after his hour in the ward. Alisia Lewandowska stood at the door at night in the autumn of 2034, when her mother had pneumonia, and did not knock. The field map gives Brodno and Siekierki the same code, S1. The register uses SZ for Brodno.
DATA.appears: Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), the register. Chapter 8: The Medic (Diana's diary of 11 October 2034, and Catalina's recording). Chapter 9: The Dendron (Protocol 003). Chapter 13: The Youngest (Alisia's recording). Chapter 16: The Protocols (Diana's last notes).
DATA.reliability: C. Six independent manuscript passages. Function, class and grid reference are from the register. The three who did not become compliant are placed at Brodno in one passage only, in Chapter 16. The count of 3 of 81 is Catalina's, in Protocol 003.

facts.function: Medical. Defensible. Multiple buildings
facts.water_condition: Class D. Stands on a low rise and has kept its feet dry. Water is carried from a cistern in the yard.
facts.events: Diana sits in the ward, 11 October 2034. Alisia stands at the door at night. The hearing in the chapel.

DATA.name: Praski (OP-P1)
DATA.summary: The market of the corridor, where trade and exchange take place.
DATA.entry: Praski. Market, trade, exchange. Class D ground. Grid reference 52.2483 N, 21.0310 E. The older project note called this place the Market. Alisia Lewandowska lists a man at Praski with a stick among those who have looked at her. She also took a tin of peaches from a man at Praski who kept a stall and whom she knew to be a crook, and left it at night on Catalina Chmielewska's dispensary shelf. The manuscript gives no other description of the post.
DATA.appears: Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), the register. Chapter 13: The Youngest (Alisia's recording).
DATA.reliability: C. Two independent manuscript passages. The register gives the function and grid reference. Alisia's recording gives the stall and the man with the stick, from a single speaker.

facts.function: Market, trade, exchange
facts.water_condition: Class D, dry but cut off.
facts.events: Alisia takes a tin of peaches from a stallholder and leaves it on Catalina's dispensary shelf.

DATA.name: Rynek, Grochów (OP-Rynek, R1)
DATA.summary: A gathering point in the middle of the corridor.
DATA.entry: Rynek (Grochów). Gathering point. Mid-corridor. Class D ground. Grid reference 52.2553 N, 21.0491 E. A diary entry is set in a room above the pharmacy. The room above the pharmacy is a long narrow loft with a sloping ceiling. A table along one wall holds five radios: two military, one shortwave, one field set Diana did not know, and one kitchen radio with a cracked case. Headphones hang on a hook, a small lamp with a green shade stands on the table, and a notebook is ruled into six columns, the sixth without a heading. Magda Wiśniewska listens here. At 23:00 the posts R0, RM, RW, RN and R4 check in, five flat voices in Russian. A woman who runs the Rynek kitchen is mentioned, and Diana comes to Rynek to ask Magda about the Kontakt rota. On a night in November Magda told Zoysa Zieliński here that a man named on the Szucha net as a consultant, with the rank of colonel, spoke with the accent of Rembertów.
DATA.appears: Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), the register. Chapter 10: The Listener (diary of 22 September 2034, the room above the pharmacy). Chapter 11: The Orphan (Diana's note on Magda, and Zoysa's recording).
DATA.reliability: C. Four independent manuscript passages. The register gives the function and grid reference. The loft and the radios are described in one diary entry, Chapter 10.

facts.function: Gathering point. Mid-corridor
facts.water_condition: Class D, dry but cut off.
facts.events: Diana spends the night of 21 to 22 September 2034 with Magda in the loft above the pharmacy. In November Magda tells Zoysa of a colonel on the Szucha net.

DATA.name: Gocławek (OP-G1)
DATA.summary: The eastern edge of the corridor, exposed, and of high value for intelligence.
DATA.entry: Gocławek. Eastern edge. Exposed. Intelligence value high. Class C ground. Grid reference 52.2357 N, 21.1246 E. Class C ground is defined in Protocol 001 as occasionally waterlogged and unpredictable. The register is the only passage in the manuscript that names Gocławek. It does not say who holds the post or what happens there.
DATA.appears: Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), section 6, Designated Positions (Survivor).
DATA.reliability: C. One manuscript passage, the register. Class, function and grid reference are as the register gives them. Nothing else in the manuscript confirms or adds to them.

facts.function: Eastern edge. Exposed. Intelligence value high

DATA.name: Mała Afryka (OP-A1)
DATA.summary: A river access point on which the corridor depends for supply.
DATA.entry: Mała Afryka. River access. Supply. Class D ground. Grid reference 52.2234 N, 21.0660 E. Class D ground is dry but cut off, and is used for survivor routes and bases. The register is the only passage in the manuscript that names Mała Afryka. It does not say what is carried through the post, or by whom.
DATA.appears: Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), section 6, Designated Positions (Survivor).
DATA.reliability: C. One manuscript passage, the register. Class, function and grid reference are as the register gives them. Nothing else in the manuscript confirms or adds to them.

facts.water_condition: Class D, dry but cut off.

DATA.name: Czerniaków (OP-Czerniaków, C1)
DATA.summary: A river outpost in the south, with the escape route running out of it.
DATA.entry: Czerniaków. River access. Escape route south. Class D ground. Grid reference 52.2221 N, 21.0478 E. The embankment is part of the outpost. Diana Antonoff was last seen here, on the night of the third flood. A document was compiled here between 23:50 on 31 December 2034 and 05:40 on 1 January 2035. On 23 October a boy pulled a crate from the water at Czerniaków which carried a label in a western language. Protocol 005 was compiled at the outpost, with a radio, a recorder, a notebook and a candle, fifteen kilometres south of Żerań. Kontakt point KC, at Mokotów and Czerniaków, watches the south near the flood margin. Diana was asked to go because a Kontakt point there had been silent for two days, and she set out on 31 December 2034. Persons crossing from Czerniaków and Wilanów are received at the Służewiec racecourse. On the embankment before dawn on 1 January 2035 it was minus 12 degrees and still, with a red glow in the north and the river ice turning from grey to pale rose. An engine without lights came slowly down the channel from the north. A Runner of about fifteen, Oliwia, left with the pouch of Diana's last pages by a culvert two hundred metres from the embankment. Diana's last diary entry breaks off in the middle of a sentence.
DATA.appears: Prologue: The Barn. Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), the register and the Kontakt points. Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), the Służewiec section. Chapter 9: The Dendron (Protocol 003), the crate of 23 October. Chapter 15: The Aftermath (Protocol 005), compiled at the outpost, and Alex's note on the last item. Chapter 16: The Protocols (the diaries of 30 December 2034 and 1 January 2035).
DATA.reliability: C. Eight independent manuscript passages. Function, class and grid reference are from the register. The night of 31 December 2034 is given in the Protocol 005 header and in Diana's last diary entry. Her fate is not stated; the entry stops.

facts.function: River access. Escape route south
facts.water_condition: Class D. Minus 12 degrees on the embankment before dawn on 1 January 2035, with the river iced.
facts.events: A crate with a western label is pulled from the water, 23 October 2034. Protocol 005 is compiled here, 31 December 2034 to 1 January 2035. Diana is last seen here, and Oliwia leaves with her last pages.

DATA.name: Siekierki (OP-SK)
DATA.summary: An exposed industrial position on the southern riverside.
DATA.entry: Siekierki. Southern riverside. Industrial. Exposed. Class B ground. Grid reference 52.2072 N, 21.0870 E. Class B ground is defined in Protocol 001 as shallow, seasonal flood, passable with knowledge. The field map gives Siekierki and Szpital (Brodno) the same code, S1. The register resolves this by using SK for Siekierki and SZ for Brodno, and notes that the field map has not been corrected. No scene is set at Siekierki.
DATA.appears: Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), section 6, Designated Positions (Survivor), and its note on the duplicated code.
DATA.reliability: C. One manuscript passage, the register, which names the post twice. Class, function and grid reference are as the register gives them.

facts.function: Southern riverside. Industrial. Exposed
facts.water_condition: Class B, shallow seasonal flood, passable with knowledge.

DATA.summary: A concealed forest position that the Runners use as a waypoint.
DATA.entry: Las. Forest. Concealed. Runner waypoint. Class D ground. Grid reference 52.1982 N, 21.1145 E. Class D ground is dry but cut off, and is used for survivor routes and bases. The register is the only passage in the manuscript that names Las. It does not say which Runners use it or on what routes.
DATA.appears: Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), section 6, Designated Positions (Survivor).

DATA.name: Przyloty (OP-P2)
DATA.summary: A position deep in the margin that can be reached only in some seasons.
DATA.entry: Przyloty. Deep in the margin. Accessibility seasonal. Class B ground. Grid reference 52.1456 N, 21.1711 E. Protocol 001 defines Class B as shallow, seasonal flood, passable with knowledge. The register gives Przyloty no function beyond its position. The same document describes the corridor as a chain of dry places joined by shallow margins that can be crossed by boat or on foot if the crossing is known, and states the rule that governs this position: what is passable in June is not passable in January. The readings for each season are provisional. No other passage in the manuscript names Przyloty, and no character is recorded as going there.
DATA.appears: Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), section 6, the register of designated positions. Sections 5 and 9 of the same Protocol give the general rules for the margins and the seasons.
DATA.reliability: E, one manuscript passage. The register states the name, class, note and grid reference with no source tag, and no other passage names the position.

facts.function: Deep in the margin. Accessibility seasonal
facts.water_condition: Class B, shallow seasonal flood. What is passable in June is not passable in January.

DATA.name: Pałac, Wilanów (OP-P3)
DATA.summary: The outpost at the southern end of the corridor, in large grounds, and a link in the escape route.
DATA.entry: Pałac (Wilanów). Southern end of the corridor. Grounds large. Escape route link. Class D ground. Grid reference 52.1653 N, 21.0897 E. It is not the Palace of Culture and Science in the centre of the city. Class D ground is dry but cut off, and serves as survivor route and base. Protocol 001 names Wilanów as the southern end of the corridor. The escape route POŁ begins here and runs south past the palace grounds, through Bielawa, toward Konstancin-Jeziorna and then east. It is about 50 km, the longest of the four routes, rural once clear of the city, and is used when the others are compromised. It takes two nights with a day lying up, 16 to 20 hours moving. In summer it is affected by southern flood levels, and its winter condition has not been recorded. The Kontakt point KP at Wilanów is listed as southern and near this outpost. Protocol 002 places the occupier's southern exit block, RKS, south of Wilanów, and says that persons who cross from Wilanów are taken to the Służewiec racecourse (estimated). In the Prologue, Alex is travelling south on the POŁ route when he meets Diana Antonoff at a farm in the grey zone.
DATA.appears: Prologue: The Barn, by the POŁ route only; the outpost is not named there. Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), sections 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9. Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), sections 3 and 6.3. Chapter 16: The Protocols, Diana's transmission of 20 June 2034, which gives Wilanów as the southern end of the corridor.
DATA.reliability: C, four passages (Protocol 001, Protocol 002, the Prologue and Chapter 16). The register itself carries no source tag.

facts.function: Southern end of the corridor. Grounds large. Escape route link
facts.water_condition: Class D, dry but cut off. The southern escape route is affected by southern flood levels in summer.
facts.events: The southern escape route, POŁ, begins here.

DATA.name: Filtry (OP-Filtry, F1)
DATA.summary: The water filtration station, and the only reliably clean supply in the corridor.
DATA.entry: Filtry. Water filtration. Critical. Near Russian R0. Class D ground. Grid reference 52.2206 N, 21.0080 E. It is the survivor position closest to the western ring. The supply is treated with charcoal and a three-stage sand bed, and it is the only supply in the corridor that is reliably free of the compound. The post at R0 has it in sight. Protocol 002 places R0 in Ochota, on the west bank and adjacent to the station, and says that every litre reaching the corridor passes under its eye. The register also lists a forward Kontakt point, KF, central and near the station, marked dangerous because it is close to the west bank. The Diana first records that the filtration is the reason the occupier has not taken the station, and then withdraws the statement: the occupier has left it alone because it is not worth taking, and the relationship runs the other way round.
DATA.appears: Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), sections 6 and 7. Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), section 4. Chapter 9: The Dendron (Protocol 003), section 6.4.
DATA.reliability: C for the position, the function and the view from R0: three documents (Protocol 001, sections 6 and 7; Protocol 002, section 4, tagged C; Protocol 003). E for the treatment and for the claim that the supply is reliably free of the compound: one passage, Protocol 003, section 6.4, untagged and Diana's own.

facts.function: Water filtration. Critical. Near Russian R0
facts.water_condition: Class D. The only supply in the corridor reliably free of the compound, treated with charcoal and a three-stage sand bed.

DATA.name: Termika (OP-Termika, the Docks)
DATA.summary: The dock outpost where the water levels of the corridor are measured.
DATA.entry: The engineer at Termika, Lucasz Kowalski, keeps a table of water levels by day. It is the only reliable series in the corridor. The staff gauge series covers the Termika and Żerań docks. Two diary entries are set at the Docks, dated 26 July 2034 and 2 September 2034. In the second flood the Dendron appeared at the Docks, where it had not been recorded before. In one flood the Docks became an island, and Lucasz stood at the main sluice gate. The control room is a concrete cube with a steel door, built as a pumping station and put to other work. It holds valves, handwheels and a hand-drawn schematic with a newer one beneath it, corrected in red. On 26 July 2034, with the staff gauge at 84.1 m, Diana Antonoff followed Lucasz through a day of inspection, and at evening a violin carried from the Zoo, about two kilometres to the south across the water. He stopped work until it ended. In the second flood the Docks overtopped at 02:50 on 2 September 2034, and the lower quay was gone by 03:15. Lucasz held the gate from 01:00 and opened the second gate at 03:40. Three people were lost: Wacław Pietrzak, 71, who kept the ferry; Iga, 23, a Runner; and a man whose name was not taken. On the night of 30 October a Russian biochemist came to the Docks and asked for the engineer.
DATA.appears: Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), section 9. Chapter 4: The Engineer, Diana's diary of 26 July 2034 and Lucasz Kowalski's recording of December 2035. Interlude: The Second Flood, Diana's diary of 2 September 2034. Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), in Alex's note that follows it. Chapter 7: The Musician. Chapter 9: The Dendron (Protocol 003), sections 4 and 10. Chapter 15: The Aftermath (Protocol 005), sections 2 and 3, for the gauge series.
DATA.reliability: The water table is the most reliable series in the corridor, by the manuscript's own account. Grade C. The Docks are named in eight passages, from Protocol 001 to Protocol 005, and two diary entries are set there. Protocol 005 rates the gauge series 0.9. The register gives no grid reference for Termika.

facts.function: Docks. The water gauge and the canal control room
facts.water_condition: Staff gauge at 84.1 m on 26 July 2034. Overtopped at 02:50 on 2 September 2034, and in one flood the Docks became an island.
facts.events: Diana follows Lucasz through a day, 26 July 2034. The second flood, 2 September 2034: three lost. A Russian biochemist asks for the engineer, 30 October 2034.

DATA.name: The Citadel
DATA.summary: The occupier's command centre, in the north of the city.
DATA.entry: The nineteenth-century fortress on the Vistula in the north of the city. Command centre. It controls river access from the north. Colonel Viktor Nikolaevich Sorokin, the commanding officer, is based here. Protocol 002 records that no excesses are attributed to him, and that a source who delivered food to his office in July found the desk clear but for a single paperback and a glass of water. At sunset each day a searchlight is turned from the Citadel to the river and passes once across the east bank, slowly, for forty seconds, and goes dark. Protocol 002 rates it the most reliable event in the corridor and calls it a statement. Alex later writes that people remember the occupation as a light and not as an event. On the night of 31 December the beam was not swept but held on Żerąń for two and a half hours from 02:30. Protocol 005 records that the mechanism of the third flood needed a sluice that could be opened from the Citadel, and that it had been prepared for a long time.
DATA.appears: Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), sections 5.1, 7.1 and 8, and Alex's note that follows it. Chapter 15: The Aftermath (Protocol 005), sections 3, 4, 5, 6 and 10.
DATA.reliability: C, two documents (Protocol 002 and Protocol 005). The searchlight at sunset is tagged C. The description of the Citadel as the command centre, and the sluice that could be opened from it, are untagged.

facts.function: Command centre. Controls river access from the north
facts.water_condition: West bank, on the higher and drier ground.
facts.events: A searchlight crosses the east bank at sunset each day. On the night of 31 December 2034 it is held on Żerań for two and a half hours from 02:30.

DATA.name: The Palace of Culture and Science
DATA.summary: A gift from Moscow, now a supply hub and the source of the broadcasts.
DATA.entry: A gift from Moscow in 1955, designed to be seen from every part of the city. It is seen from every part of the city. It is now a logistics and supply hub, and it carries a mast from which broadcasts are made, in Russian and in Polish. The loudspeaker transcript of Magda Wiśniewska comes from these broadcasts. The broadcast studio is in the Palace. Studio Two is on the eighth floor, and the announcer is kept in a room on the nineteenth with a lock on the outside and a view over the roofs of Śródmieście. The corridors carry a carpet in red and gold laid in 1955. Protocol 002 gives the loudspeaker at 08:00 and 20:00, from the Palace and the Old Town together. Interlude IV gives the script four readings a day, at 08:00, 12:00, 18:00 and 20:00, with a shorter form on the half hour at night, over a network of two thousand speakers. The headnote to Interlude I calls the transcript the Palace loudspeaker, and Wiktor Szeliga hears it from Block C, two and a half kilometres away. An informant also passed the Brigade the state of the fuel stocks at the Palace in winter.
DATA.appears: Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), sections 5.2 and 8. Interlude I: Wiktor Szeliga, Block C. Interlude IV: The Voice, Studio Two. Interlude VI: Wiktor Szeliga, Shelter 9, which gives the same words and voice from a fitting in a hall on the left bank and does not name the Palace. Chapter 11: The Orphan, in Zoysa's recording of February 2036.
DATA.reliability: C, five passages. The Palace as the seat of the broadcasts is given in Protocol 002 and in the headnote to Interlude I. The studio in the building rests on Interlude IV alone, a reconstruction from a script, an engineer's log and recordings. The fuel stocks rest on one recording.

facts.function: Logistics and supply hub. Broadcast mast and studio
facts.water_condition: West bank, on the higher and drier ground.
facts.events: Loudspeaker broadcasts at 08:00 and 20:00, with the Old Town.

apps.t: Interlude I: Wiktor Szeliga, Block C
Interlude IV: The Voice, Studio Two

DATA.name: The Old Town and the Royal Castle
DATA.summary: A rebuilt district, occupied for its symbolism.
DATA.entry: Rebuilt after 1944 from photographs and paintings. Occupied for its symbolism. Loudspeakers stand on the ramparts. Protocol 001 lists the Old Town among the districts of the west bank, which stands on higher ground and is drier and occupied. Protocol 002 gives the loudspeaker at 08:00 and 20:00 from the Old Town and the Palace together. The broadcasts speak of order, restored services and warm beds, in a woman's pleasant voice, and do not mention the water. In Protocol 005 Diana returns to the rebuilding: the city was rebuilt from photographs and paintings after 1944, Warsaw is proud of it, and Fritha Cielinski has several thousand photographs. Diana makes no further comment.
DATA.appears: Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), section 4. Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), sections 5.3 and 8. Chapter 15: The Aftermath (Protocol 005), section 6, where the rebuilding of the city is noted and the Old Town is not named.
DATA.reliability: C, three passages. The loudspeakers are tagged C in Protocol 002. The occupation of the district for its symbolism is Diana's judgement, untagged.

facts.function: Occupied for its symbolism. Loudspeakers on the ramparts
facts.water_condition: West bank, on the higher and drier ground.
facts.events: Loudspeaker broadcasts at 08:00 and 20:00, with the Palace.

DATA.name: The Saxon Garden and Łazienki
DATA.summary: Open ground that the occupier has turned to air defence.
DATA.entry: Open ground turned to air defence. Missile batteries have been seen between the trees. Protocol 002 counts it among five places of consequence on the west bank, which is drier than the east and held by the occupier with ease. The report is a single sighting. It does not say which of the two parks holds the batteries, or how many, and no other passage in the manuscript names either park. It is the only air defence recorded in the manuscript.
DATA.appears: Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), section 5.4.
DATA.reliability: U, one manuscript passage, which tags the sighting itself as one source.

facts.function: Air defence. Missile batteries seen between the trees
facts.water_condition: West bank, drier than the east.

DATA.name: Szucha and Pawiak
DATA.summary: Two buildings of interrogation and imprisonment that the occupier has taken over unchanged.
DATA.entry: The German security police took the building at Aleja Szucha 25 in 1939 and used its cellars for interrogation. The Russian force has reoccupied it. A tunnel is reported to run from the cellars to the old prison at Pawiak, which has been reactivated. Persons are taken in. Some are returned. A source who walked past Pawiak on 14 September counted seven lit windows. In each case the occupier has built nothing. Szucha was built to be afraid of. Pawiak was built to hold. Major Alexei Dmitrievich Budanov, head of screening and intelligence, operates from Szucha, and his name is on the orders. Interlude III is set in the building. The bedroom is on the third floor of the north wing and the office is room 214, with a plaster rose on the ceiling. A courtyard has a plane tree. The screening room is on the lower ground floor, was a cell, and has a drain in its rubber floor. Screening runs in seven steps and ends in one of four decisions: release, retain, transfer or treat. In Chapter 10 Magda Wiśniewska says that she gave the occupier eleven names as a child, that four of those people were taken to Szucha, and that two returned. Szucha is also the name of a radio net that Magda monitors. Pawiak is named in no passage other than Protocol 002.
DATA.appears: Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), sections 5.5 and 7.2. Interlude III: Major Budanov, Aleja Szucha. Chapter 10: The Listener, Magda Wiśniewska's recording of March 2036. Chapter 11: The Orphan, Diana's diary of 30 November 2034, on the Szucha net. Chapter 12: The Codex (Protocol 004), the intercept from the Szucha net.
DATA.reliability: C for Szucha as the seat of Budanov and of screening: Protocol 002, Interlude III, Chapter 10, Chapter 11 and Protocol 004. U for the tunnel, one source, as Protocol 002 tags it. Pawiak is named in one passage only, Protocol 002, section 5.5, which says without a tag that it has been reactivated and gives one source's count of seven lit windows on 14 September.

facts.function: Interrogation, screening and imprisonment
facts.water_condition: West bank, on the higher and drier ground.
facts.events: Seven lit windows counted at Pawiak, 14 September 2034. Interlude III follows one day of screening here.

apps.t: Interlude III: Major Budanov, Aleja Szucha

DATA.name: R0 and RM
DATA.summary: Two Russian posts on the water, one of which watches the filtration station.
DATA.entry: RM stands about three kilometres from the Żerań dock and can be seen from the roof of the control room on a clear morning. It has not fired. R0 is the post that matters to the water. The filtration station at Filtry stands within sight of it, and every litre that reaches the corridor passes under its eye. R0 is also the call sign under which the rota is read on the observation net. From the observation post a rota is read aloud every sixth day, at 06:00, to six field commanders, who each reply Received and a number. R0 stands in Ochota, on the west bank, adjacent to Filtry. RM stands at Tarchomin, north of Żerąń, and puts direct pressure on the hub; its coordinates are given as approximate. Protocol 002 records a radio check of all posts every four hours, on the hour. On 22 September 2034 Magda Wiśniewska let Diana hear five posts check in at 23:00: R0, RM, RW, RN and R4. On the night of 31 December, Kontakt KB reported many engines to the north, at RM. Interlude II is set in the observation post: a room four metres by three, in cinder block, with a steel shutter raised twenty centimetres over a strip of the city. Through it Sasha Lebedev sees an eleven-storey block whose lower four floors are covered by green growth advancing four to nine centimetres a day. He had been at the post ninety-four days on 4 October and was relieved on 11 October. The survivors call him the Watcher.
DATA.appears: Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), section 6, where Filtry is listed as near R0. Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), sections 4, 7.3, 8 and 11.1. Interlude II: Sasha Lebedev, Observation Post R0. Chapter 10: The Listener, Diana's diary of 22 September 2034. Chapter 15: The Aftermath (Protocol 005), section 3, for RM.
DATA.reliability: C for R0: four documents (Protocol 001, Protocol 002, Interlude II and Chapter 10). E for RM: three passages (Protocol 002, Chapter 10 and Protocol 005), and its coordinates are marked approximate.

facts.function: Observation posts. R0 watches Filtry; RM presses on the Żerań hub
facts.events: The 06:00 transmission from R0 stops for four minutes, 2 October 2034. Sasha Lebedev is relieved, 11 October 2034. Many engines reported at RM on the night of 31 December 2034.

apps.t: Interlude II: Sasha Lebedev, Observation Post R0

DATA.name: SP-1, Marymont
DATA.summary: A screening point in the north, in a sports academy.
DATA.entry: The sports halls and halls of residence of the physical education academy on Marymoncka, on the left bank opposite Białołęka. It receives persons who cross in the north. Two buses a day come along the Marymoncka road, one at about 07:00 and one at about 16:00. They arrive with the blinds down and leave with the blinds up. What is done in the halls is not known. The lights are on. Protocol 002 gives its position as approximately 52.272 N, 20.962 E. It is one of at least four points west of the Vistula, each marked SP in black stencil on the leaflets and on the buses. The bus times are the count of one Runner who works the northern reach, and the Protocol marks them as estimated. The compiler had no source who had been through a screening point and returned willing to say what is done there. The observations were made from the east bank between 3 September and 20 October 2034.
DATA.appears: Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), section 6 (the screening camps), section 6.1, and the table of screening points that follows section 6.6.
DATA.reliability: E. One manuscript passage (Protocol 002, section 6.1, repeated in its table). The bus count rests on one Runner. No second witness and no one who has been inside.

facts.function: Screening point, in the physical education academy
facts.water_condition: Left bank.
facts.events: Two buses a day, at about 07:00 and 16:00, observed 3 September to 20 October 2034.

DATA.name: SP-2, Torwar
DATA.summary: A screening point in an ice arena at the centre.
DATA.entry: The ice arena and sports hall on Łazienkowska, near the river, in the centre. It receives persons who cross at the central bridges. The lights are on all night. The ice is said to be still kept frozen, and the power for it was the first restored in that district. That is a large use of power for a place that offers warm beds. Protocol 002 gives its position as approximately 52.216 N, 21.040 E. The report of the ice and the power comes from one source, who worked the south shore before the second flood. Interlude III: Major Budanov, Aleja Szucha, describes a checkpoint on the Poniatowski Bridge, where arrivals are assessed on the bridge and passed on to a reception hall on the left bank. The manuscript does not say whether that hall is this arena.
DATA.appears: Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), section 6.2 and the table of screening points. Interlude III: Major Budanov, Aleja Szucha, for the bridge checkpoint.
DATA.reliability: E for the crossings and the position. U for the ice and the power: one source. One manuscript passage (Protocol 002, section 6.2, repeated in its table), with no second witness.

facts.function: Screening point, in the ice arena on Łazienkowska

apps.t: Interlude III: Major Budanov, Aleja Szucha

DATA.name: SP-3, Służewiec
DATA.summary: A screening point at the racecourse, the only one with its own fence.
DATA.entry: The racecourse in Mokotów: stables, a grandstand and a very large open ground. It receives persons who cross from Czerniaków and Wilanów, in the south. It is the only point with a fence of its own. The fence is new, two and a half metres high, in pale galvanised wire that shows against the grass in photographs taken from the flood margin. Persons are queued on the open ground, and the queue is said to be orderly. Protocol 002 gives its position as approximately 52.185 N, 20.970 E. Mokotów is on the west bank, on the higher and drier ground. Of the three points the compiler can place, it is the only one for which Protocol 002 cites photographs.
DATA.appears: Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), section 6.3 and the table of screening points.
DATA.reliability: C for the fence: two photographs. E for the crossings and the position. U for the queue, which is hearsay. One manuscript passage (Protocol 002, section 6.3, repeated in its table).

facts.function: Screening point at the racecourse. The only one with its own fence
facts.water_condition: West bank, on the higher and drier ground.

DATA.name: SP-4
DATA.summary: A fourth screening point, known by its number only.
DATA.entry: The location of SP-4 is not known. It is known by its number only, from a bus destination board seen on the embankment road. Protocol 002 states that there are at least four screening points, all west of the Vistula, and gives this sighting as the reason it says at least four. Its table lists the point as not placed, with the crossings it receives from and its coordinates both not known.
DATA.appears: Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), sections 6 and 6.4, and the table of screening points.
DATA.reliability: U. One manuscript passage (Protocol 002, section 6.4): one sighting of one bus destination board, with no second witness.

facts.function: Screening point

DATA.name: Okęcie
DATA.summary: The airport, a supply hub and the subject of a rumour.
DATA.entry: The airport is not a screening point. It is the supply hub, and it is where the aircraft come. Among survivors it is believed that certain persons are not sent on to the shelters at all but are flown out from Okęcie, and that they are the persons the occupier most wishes to keep. The word used is rendered. The belief has been heard in three places that do not speak to one another. Protocol 002 also lists the airport among the posts of the outer ring as RA, Chopin Airport, with the purpose supply hub and air control, at approximately 52.166 N, 20.967 E. It uses RA for the airport and RKS for the post south of Wilanów, to resolve two codes the field map gives twice. In Protocol 001 no route west can be made, because of the airport and the occupied west bank, and three attempts were abandoned. In Protocol 004, link WT-05 of the evidence chain is the route of a single supply flight into the airport, flown three times at night with no declared cargo, and is rated 0.6.
DATA.appears: Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), sections 3 and 6.5. Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), section 4. Chapter 12: The Codex (Protocol 004), section 7, link WT-05.
DATA.reliability: C for the airport as a supply hub: Protocol 002 and the supply flight at link WT-05 of Protocol 004. U for the rendering: heard in three places, seen by no source. Three manuscript passages.

facts.function: Supply hub and air control
facts.events: A supply flight with no declared cargo is flown three times at night (Protocol 004, link WT-05).

DATA.name: The shelters
DATA.summary: Numbered places in the west where those screened are said to be sent.
DATA.entry: The shelters are numbered. Persons who pass a screening point are sent on to them. Shelters 1 to 6 were heard of in 2034. The numbers rise: Interlude VI, in June 2035, is set in Shelter 9, a former sports hall on the left bank. The offer of them is made every day, by loudspeaker and by leaflet. The leaflet is a single A5 sheet with a photograph of a bed, and the voice says that the shelters on the left bank are open and that there are beds. Protocol 002 counts about 340 persons as having accepted the offer since June 2034. Shelter 9 is a hall forty-two metres by twenty-four, with 260 camp beds in rows of ten, each with a numbered grey blanket. The washroom is the old changing room, with twenty-four basins. The loudspeaker is on the wall above the double doors and is much louder than on the east bank. The warden, Pan Cichocki, a retired surveyor, keeps an intake ledger that sorts each person into one of five categories. The lights go down to a third at 22:00. A hum from the vent below the scoreboard, once in six seconds, is noted once in the ledger margin. Alex marks in the text which details he has supplied himself. He has asked in four shelters and does not know what became of Wiktor Szeliga.
DATA.appears: Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), sections 6.6 and 9.3. Interlude I: Wiktor Szeliga, Block C (the leaflet and the loudspeaker). Interlude IV: The Voice, Studio Two (the script). Interlude VI: Wiktor Szeliga, Shelter 9.
DATA.reliability: E. Four manuscript passages (Protocol 002, section 6.6; Interlude I; Interlude IV; Interlude VI). Shelters 1 to 6 are U, heard from two persons who were not together. Shelter 9 rests on one ledger, and Alex marks which details of the hall are his own reconstruction.

facts.function: Beds for those who pass screening
facts.water_condition: Left bank.
facts.events: About 340 persons accept the offer from June 2034. Wiktor Szeliga is in Shelter 9 in June 2035.

apps.t: Interlude I: Wiktor Szeliga, Block C
Interlude IV: The Voice, Studio Two

DATA.name: Escape routes
DATA.summary: The gaps in the occupier's ring through which survivors leave.
DATA.entry: The outer ring is not a wall. It is a series of eyes with gaps between them, and the gaps are the escape routes. No post is held in strength greater than a company. The occupier knows where the gaps are, and Diana Antonoff believes it has left them open because it prefers to watch what passes through. The route from Czerniaków runs south, and the palace at Wilanów is a link in it. The most direct route passes close to a Russian post and is high risk. In winter, when the water is frozen, there is a winter route, which the Runners use. Protocol 001, section 8, tabulates four routes. The north route, the most direct and the preferred route over ice in winter, is 25 km, through the gap between the posts RN and R2, past the Kontakt point KB toward Nieporęt. It takes one night on foot, seven to nine hours, or about four hours across the ice in deep winter, and in summer it is high risk. The north-east route passes wide of the post at Kobyłka toward Pustelnik, 45 km, with woodland cover, and is called the safest and the one used to move high-value persons. The eastern route, 30 km past the Kontakt points KJ and KW and south through Józefów, is the everyday route and the most monitored. The southern route runs 50 km from the palace at Wilanów through Bielawa toward Konstancin-Jeziorna, and is used when the others are compromised. No route leads west, because of the airport and the occupied west bank.
DATA.appears: Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), sections 4, 6, 8 and 9, and Alex's note that follows it. Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), section 3.
DATA.reliability: E. Four manuscript passages (Protocol 001, sections 4, 8 and 9; Protocol 002, section 3), all by one compiler. The routes, distances and durations are her estimates. That the occupier leaves the gaps open is Diana Antonoff's belief, and no source confirms it.

facts.function: Routes out of the corridor, through the gaps in the occupier's ring
facts.water_condition: Seasonal. The north route is high risk in summer and the preferred route over ice in winter. The southern route is affected by southern flood levels in summer.
facts.events: Three attempts at a route west were abandoned.

DATA.name: The sewers
DATA.summary: The tunnels under the city, used as a way through in 1944 and again now.
DATA.entry: The sewers are a way through the city. In August 1944 a unit of the Home Army moved through the sewers under Śródmieście. In the present account Anna carried the child Nikita down to the sewers, because that was where one went, and the two travelled through them for three weeks. Nikita, at six, was the best ear in the tunnels. The Dendron has been found in the sewers of Targówek. A mass in a sewer does not remove its function but blocks it, so that the drains back up and the water rises. The account of 1944 is a story that Marek Olszewski tells at the kitchen table on Thursdays, which Diana Antonoff records in her diary of 30 November 2034. The unit's captain held his line for three weeks, and the men later found in his coat a note offering him terms. The account of the three weeks is Nikita's own, written on a pad in Wrocław in February 2036, when she is eight. Anna was thirteen. In the dark Nikita could hear the water in the pipe, people breathing far off and boots overhead, and she signalled to Anna with her fingers on Anna's wrist. She also heard a low sound in the pipes, like a person crying with a hand over the mouth, and it did not frighten her.
DATA.appears: Chapter 9: The Dendron (Protocol 003), section 4. Chapter 11: The Orphan (Diana's diary of 30 November 2034, with Marek's story of the captain). Chapter 14: The Mouse (Nikita's written account).
DATA.reliability: C for the Dendron in the sewers of Targówek: Protocol 003 marks it as several sources. E for the rest: three manuscript passages, each a single telling. The 1944 story is Marek's, and the three weeks are Nikita's, written at eight about events at six.

facts.function: A way through the city, under it
facts.water_condition: Where the Dendron blocks a drain, the water backs up and rises.
facts.events: A Home Army unit moves through the sewers under Śródmieście, August 1944. Anna and Nikita spend three weeks in them.

DATA.name: St Michael's Cathedral
DATA.summary: A flooded cathedral on the Praga shore.
DATA.entry: The cathedral stands on the Praga side of the water and the water has been in it. A tide line runs across the nave pillars at the height of a hip. The roof is open in two places over the north aisle. Pigeons nest there, and there is a smell of wet plaster and old incense. The west door hangs from one hinge. The diary entry is dated 9 August 2034, at 06:15, under overcast and low light, with the water flat and the colour of pewter. Diana stands for a full minute inside the west door to let her eyes find the dark. The nave holds several thousand photographs, laid in rows on the altar steps and along the lowest courses of the pews, each weighted at the corners with a pebble or a spent cartridge, and more are pegged on lines between the pillars. They are sorted by year: weddings in one aisle, holidays in another, school photographs in a long rank. Felicyta Cielinski, nineteen, sits among them on a folding stool and talks to the prints. A child of about six, Nikita, sits on the floor and touches none. A Runner stays at the door and will not come in. In her own testimony Fritha calls the place the church, gives the count as five thousand, and says she brought the prints in by boat and laid them on the steps. Alex notes in Chapter 3 that Fritha's church is in Class D, under the name of a place that was a cathedral.
DATA.appears: Chapter 2: The Photographer, in Diana's diary of 9 August 2034 (SY/FC/0011_DD, headed the Praga shoreline, vicinity St Michael's Cathedral) and in Fritha's recorded testimony (SY/FC/0001_GR). Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), Alex's note that follows the Protocol.
DATA.reliability: C that Fritha kept her prints in a flooded church on the Praga shore: Diana's diary and Fritha's testimony agree. E for the state of the building: one observer, Diana, on 9 August 2034. Three manuscript passages. Only the diary names St Michael's.

facts.function: Fritha's church, where she keeps the photographs
facts.water_condition: Flooded. A tide line runs across the nave pillars at hip height.
facts.events: Diana's first visit, 9 August 2034 at 06:15. On the twenty-second day Fritha photographs Diana.

DATA.name: Wetlands & Houseboat
DATA.summary: The still water at the north of the corridor where Diana lived.
DATA.entry: Diana Antonoff lived alone on an abandoned houseboat moored at Żerań, at the northern edge of the wetlands, where the water ran quietest. Her diary entries are headed with the date, the place, the weather and the state of the water. Many are set on the deck and in the cabin of the houseboat. The houseboat is an hour or more on foot from the outpost, by way of the one bridge the community holds, though it can be seen across the water. It lies low on the near bank among willow, reed and broad pale leaves, and a passer-by at twenty metres would not know a hull was there. One other boat is moored further along. From the deck the red and white chimneys of the power plant stand across the canal, and at night the hum of the plant carries over. When Diana first goes aboard on 1 June 2034 the cabin has a cup on its side, a calendar left on a month long past, and a folding settee with a worn cover. The canal in summer has reeds, lily pads, a beaver and dragonflies, which Protocol 001 records in its notes. On 9 December the canal ice is walkable at the margin, and by 28 December it is frozen from bank to bank. Diana's last entries are written from the deck on 30 December 2034. The Foreword records that she disappeared from Czerniaków on the night of the third flood, and the houseboat could not be reached afterwards.
DATA.appears: Foreword. Diary 001: The Arrival (1 June 2034). Chapter 1: The Blasphemer (diary of 14 June 2034, in the wetlands). Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), section 9 and the notes to file. Interlude: The Second Flood (diary of 28 August 2034). Chapter 15: The Aftermath (Protocol 005), Alex's closing note. Chapter 16: The Protocols (the dispatch of 20 June 2034 and the diaries of 9, 28 and 30 December 2034).
DATA.reliability: C. Stated by Alex in the Foreword, and confirmed by the headings and text of Diana's diary entries from Diary 001 onward. At least eight manuscript passages.

facts.function: Diana's home, an abandoned houseboat
facts.water_condition: Still water at the northern edge of the wetlands. The canal ice is walkable at the margin on 9 December and frozen bank to bank by 28 December 2034.
facts.events: Diana goes aboard, 1 June 2034. Her last entries are written from the deck, 30 December 2034.

DATA.name: Żerań power station
DATA.summary: A power station on which the Dendron does not grow.
DATA.entry: The Dendron does not grow on the bricks of the Żerań power station. Diana Antonoff, who compiled Protocol 003, has no explanation and examined it on four days. The organism grows up to the edge of the old coal yard and stops. It is a note to file, not a finding. From the houseboat across the canal the chimneys of the plant are striped red and white, and the hum of the plant carries at night. The log in Protocol 005 records that the station basement flooded and the lights at Żerań went out at 02:05 on 1 January 2035, and that eleven rounds were fired at 02:40 at the chimney, the control room and the dock. Radio contact with the Żerań station ended at 03:05 in the middle of the sentence "Tell Diana the chimney is". Alex later finds the red and white stack standing, the only thing at Żerań not brought down, with reeds grown up around it and a heron at its foot, and does not know why it was spared.
DATA.appears: Chapter 9: The Dendron (Protocol 003), section 11.1. Diary 001: The Arrival (the plant seen from the houseboat). Chapter 15: The Aftermath (Protocol 005), the log of 1 January 2035, section 5, section 10.3 and Alex's closing note.
DATA.reliability: E for the bricks: one manuscript passage (Protocol 003, section 11.1), examined by Diana Antonoff on four days, with no cause given and no second witness. C for the shelling and the loss of power: the Protocol 005 log, its section 5 and Alex's closing note agree. Four passages in all.

facts.function: Power station
facts.water_condition: The basement flooded on 1 January 2035.
facts.events: On 1 January 2035 the lights go out at 02:05, eleven rounds are fired at 02:40 and radio contact ends at 03:05. The chimney is not brought down.

DATA.name: The Zone
DATA.summary: The Russian research programme under which the surviving population of Warsaw was held as a test cohort.
DATA.entry: Neural Harvest is the name of a research programme described in an operational brief that Diana Antonoff received on 28 December, through the Russian scientist she calls a source in Protocol 003. The brief is eleven pages, in Russian and in English, on the stationery of a research directorate, stamped and numbered. Hers was copy 3 of 5. The brief treats the survivors of the Warsaw corridor, estimated at forty thousand, as a test cohort. It treats the flood as the delivery system. It records the effects of the organism as behavioural endpoints in four stages and names stage 4 as the target state. The brief names loss of containment as the principal risk to the programme, and loss of the measurement through the emergence of an organised population as the secondary risk. It considers both low. A small proportion of the cohort is expected to show atypical resistance. Such subjects are to be identified, monitored and recorded. They are not to be removed from the cohort unless they affect the integrity of the measurement. The target for the cohort phase is that not less than 60 per cent of the cohort is assessed at stage 3 or above within 90 days of the establishment of continuous exposure. The phase ends when the Directorate determines that the measurement is complete. Results are held in a joint repository and are to be shared with the partner establishments on completion of the cohort phase. The brief gives ethical review as not applicable and states no reason. The name comes from the observation section: a harvest is the gathering of what has grown. The brief is reproduced as Appendix: The Brief, with the names of the Western partners and the initials withheld. It lists four annexes: A, the organism; B, delivery; C, behavioural endpoints; and D, observation, cordon and data. They are in the binder and are not reproduced. The programme is described as joint, run by the Russian state and at least two Western states through their agencies, military research establishments and private biotechnology contractors. The Russians supplied the organism and the Western partners supplied the means of enhancing it, stabilising it in a water supply and optimising it. The brief gives the grounds for the choice of city as isolated, contained and non-attributable, with no external access and no prospect of relief. The scientist gave Diana the name on 30 October 2034, and she wrote it in the second binder, not in Protocol 003. She believes the cohort phase ended with the destruction of Żerań on 1 January 2035, and rates that belief 0.6. In Interlude V an account lead works on a contract called the Programme, whose name has two words, one suggesting the brain and one a verb for gathering a crop.

DATA.name: Diana Antonoff
DATA.summary: Ukrainian journalist, aged 28, who documented the survivor community and assembled the Protocols. Disappeared on the night of the third flood.
DATA.entry: Diana Antonoff was a Ukrainian journalist who filed dispatches to Suspilne. She lived alone on an abandoned houseboat moored at Żerań, at the northern edge of the wetlands, where the others said the water ran quietest. She disappeared from the survivor outpost at Czerniaków on the night of the third flood, in the first January of the occupation's seventh year. She was twenty-eight. Her last dispatch was filed a fortnight before. No body was recovered and no statement was issued. The community she had documented entered her name among the missing and continued the work she had taught them. She is the source of the Codex marks and of the recorded testimonies. A nine-minute tape of her voice survives and is used once in the archive. She entered the corridor on 1 June 2034, by reed boat before first light, having crossed the grey zone alone. Alex met her once, for half an hour, at a farm south of the city shortly before she went in, where she ate energy gels from a sachet and carried a brick of camera batteries wrapped in cloth. Interlude I describes her at twenty-eight as small and dark, her Polish careful and foreign. She opened every diary page in the same order: date, place, conditions, temperature, pressure and flood level. She wrote her notes against each transcript in pencil. She compiled all five Protocols. Her last diary entry, written at OP-Czerniaków on 1 January 2035 under the heading of the third flood, stops in mid-sentence. In it she gives the pouch of final pages to a Runner, tells her that she will follow, and records that this was untrue. The safe on the houseboat held a camera, a spare battery, the key to the boat and a small framed photograph whose description matches the print that Fritha took of her. The manuscript does not say whether she lived. The Foreword says only that if she is alive, she has chosen not to be found.

DATA.name: Goya Liszka
DATA.summary: Veteran of Mariupol and the Runners' guide through the wetlands. Swears without pause. Hears drones before anyone else.
DATA.entry: Goya Liszka served in the last cellar at Mariupol, under what had been a bakery. Ten men held it. Nine died when a shell came through. He was at the back of the room and lay three days among the dead because to move was to be heard. No camp or column would take him afterwards, because he does not sleep and watches the door. The Zone took him because it asked only what he could do. He can hear a drone in the air before anyone lifts a head, and he reads a man's route from the mud on his boots. He knows where every Runner in the wetlands is at any hour, and which chimneys at Żerań still carry a watcher. He swears at everything: the boat, the sky, the dead, God, his own hands. Diana records him as the most damaged person she had met in the Zone and the most necessary. He speaks to children and drones in the same voice. In the ward at Brodno he called Pawel "the banker" and told him to count a Runner's blood on the floor, and was told by Catalina that he was bleeding on her floor, which he was. He stood at the door when Lucasz was locked in the control room. In 2036 he lives at a veterans' facility outside Gdańsk, a former sanatorium with long glassed corridors, and sits in every room with his back to the wall. Alex reached him only by saying that he had been to see Janek, at which the swearing stopped. On the dock at Żerań Goya cursed God for ten minutes in front of Janek, who called it an honest prayer, and the two have sat together since. On the night of the second flood, 2 September 2034, he had the Runners out by 01:45, twenty-three children in four boats, and all twenty-three came back. He says that in all the years none of his has been taken. He took Zoysa to the range when she arrived at fifteen, and did not speak to her for four days after she told him what she had kept from him. Diana noted that he did not swear at Janek.

DATA.name: Felicyta "Fritha" Cielinski
DATA.summary: Aged 19. Keeps photographs. Found in a church in Class D ground.
DATA.entry: Fritha Cielinski was nineteen when Diana met her. A Runner at the door, who would not come in, gave her name and said only that the girl in the church was not to be hurried. Her church stands in Class D ground, under the name of a place that was a cathedral. She keeps photographs. Forty-one prints came out of the water in her father's jacket, which she found on a railing six days afterwards, caught by the sleeve. She dried them on a radiator in a stairwell without power. The emulsion had lifted and her mother's face had slid a little to the left. Her account is that photographs do not keep people. They keep a version of the light that fell on someone, and a person who has made a photograph into a god has nothing else to pray to. She was nineteen when Diana told her that a photograph is a promise to remember and not the memory itself, and she thought it the most unfair thing anyone had said to her. She still thinks so, but she looks at people while they are in the room. Alex met her in Berlin in November 2035, when she was twenty or twenty-one. She works in the basement of a museum, in a long room kept at eighteen degrees, restoring recordings and glass negatives in white cotton gloves, and she would not be photographed. In a plan chest drawer she keeps found prints in glassine sleeves, at least a hundred and ninety, each row marked Unclaimed, and says that in two years no one has looked. In the church at Praga the prints lay in rows on the altar steps and hung from lines between the pillars, sorted by year and weighted with pebbles or spent cartridges, and she spoke to them as to people. Diana visited every second day for three weeks, and on the twenty-second day Fritha agreed to photograph her. She kept the negative. The framed print in Diana's safe, of a woman on a shoreline looking at the water, matches that photograph. Nikita stayed with her through most of that autumn, and Fritha gave her the one print she never boxed.

facts.distinguishing_trait: Keeps photographs, and will not be photographed.
facts.fate: Alive in 2036, restoring recordings and glass negatives in a museum basement in Berlin.

DATA.name: Janek Dąbrowski
DATA.summary: Wanderer. Lodged with Rosa and Marek. Spiritual anchor of the community.
DATA.entry: Janek Dąbrowski came to rest in October. In September Rosa Olszewska offered him the empty back room of the third-floor flat in Białołęka that she shared with Marek. The room had a window, a bed with a real mattress, a wool blanket and a stove, and had been empty since the winter. His account of the offer is that it is not a sin to want to be kept, and that the rule, if there is one, is not that a person must not want but that a person must not want what belongs to someone else and call it theirs. The room was Rosa's to give, not to keep. He was fifty-five in August 2034 and fifty-seven when Alex met him. He studied for the priesthood and left it to marry, and his wife died of cancer five years before the invasion. He has owned since then a coat, a pair of boots and a prayer book. Diana met him on 19 August 2034 on the dock at Żerań, sitting beside Goya in a silence that the two took turns to keep. He asked her nothing, and she said aloud that she had not prayed in two years. He told her that the city is in God, and not the other way about. It was Diana who asked him, in the doorway of the room, whether he could not have it or did not think he was allowed. His wife was Hanna, and they were married for twenty-three years in a small flat in Praga with a green table that had one short leg and a folded beer mat under it. In January 2036 Alex found him at a refugee centre outside Przemyśl, a converted barracks, where he makes tea and at four each afternoon walks a round of the doors with a steel flask and four paper cups. He keeps a room two doors from the kitchen for anyone who cannot sleep near others breathing, and strips the bed in the morning. He says that he still believes, in a smaller form than before.

DATA.name: Lucasz Kowalski
DATA.summary: Engineer who runs the control room. Locked in it for seven hours by his friends.
DATA.entry: Lucasz Kowalski is the engineer of the community's systems. He reads the gauge at the dock and keeps the control room. Artur told Tanja that the engineer had a fault and that she was the only thing that could fix it. On a Thursday in late October a group arranged for Lucasz to be locked in the control room: Artur took the key from his belt, Goya stood at the door with folded arms and told him to sit down, and Diana neither took part nor stopped it. The door did not open for seven hours. On the night of the pressure fall his reading of the dock gauge at 18:00, up fourteen centimetres on the morning, was relayed to Diana by Artur, who ran. Diana's diary of 26 July 2034 places him at OP-Termika, the Docks: a man of about thirty-six in a canvas jacket gone white at the seams, who laid the flat of his hand on forty-three objects in one day before he spoke a figure. The control room is a concrete cube with valves, handwheels and a schematic corrected in red. Before the war he was a civil engineer on the Vistula Canal, a relief scheme. He wrote its gate sequence, and the occupiers took the control room and ran it in reverse, so that the canal brought the water into the city. When the violin sounded from the Zoo he stopped where he stood. On 2 September 2034 he stood at the main gate from 01:00 and opened the second gate at 03:40. At 01:20 on 1 January 2035 he sent his last transmission from Żerań: the occupiers had swapped the same two lines. In December 2035 Alex found him on a sluice site on the Martwa Wisła outside Gdańsk, where the work stops at four on Fridays and he takes off his hat.

DATA.reliability: C (6). His own recording, Diana's diary of 26 July 2034 and Protocol 005 agree on the Vistula Canal and the reversed gate sequence. The occupiers' takeover is hearsay in Diana's diary and is confirmed by his own account. His age of about 36 is Diana's estimate.

DATA.name: Tanja Dopolewka
DATA.summary: Aged 36. Violinist who teaches a mixed class of survivors.
DATA.entry: Tanja Dopolewka was thirty-six, small and square-shouldered, in a man's cardigan. By every account the archivist was given she had been one of the best violinists in Warsaw. She ran a room on the second floor with a piano, a carpet and a row of small plastic chairs. On the Saturday of the visit eight people were present, aged between nine and seventy, each holding an instrument. She taught with the words "Again" and "Listen to her, not to yourself". When a boy of eleven dropped his bow, a black carbon-fibre bow with white hair, she went still for about three seconds, as a person does who hears their name spoken in another room, then returned it to his hand and said "Again". The class meets in a former school in Wrocław that now holds the city's reconstruction fund. Alex visited in January 2036, and she had set one condition in writing: no questions about the soldier. Her instrument store, once the school's chemistry laboratory, holds about ninety instruments, each with a luggage label in her hand, and a rack of some thirty bows made by their players from cane, bamboo, a curtain rail, a ski pole, ash, hazel and green willow. In her own account she taught at the Academy in Warsaw, was twenty-eight when the city fell, and kept its basement open for four years. In a winter four years into the occupation a young soldier came into her studio at night, and she killed him. The carbon bow broke in the struggle and she left it behind. In the Zone she played most evenings in the old lion house at the Zoo, on an upturned feed bin, with a bow of stripped green willow strung with horsehair. Diana's diary of 17 November 2034 records three of Catalina's patients weeping at the violin, and Lucasz standing at the back.
DATA.appears: Foreword (described, not named); Chapter 4: The Engineer (as the violin, in Diana's diary of 26 July 2034 and Lucasz's recording); Chapter 7: The Musician (Alex's visit, Diana's diary of 17 November 2034, and her recording); Chapter 14: The Mouse (in Alex's introduction and Nikita's recording)
DATA.reliability: C (4). Observed directly by Alex in 2036, described in Diana's diary of 17 November 2034, and told in her own recording and in Lucasz's. Her age of 36 agrees with her statement that she was 28 when Warsaw fell.

DATA.name: Catalina Chmielewska
DATA.summary: Medic who runs the clinic. Aged 40 at first account, 41 later.
DATA.entry: Before the war Catalina Chmielewska was a software engineer in Warsaw, at a firm that made scheduling systems for hospitals. After the invasion she trained as a volunteer medic. She came to the Zone from Kraków eighteen months before Diana met her at Brodno in the second week of October 2034. In the Zone she ran the old hospital at Brodno. In 2036 she runs a clinic in Kraków from a former bank, using the vault for stores. People called her selfless. Her rule for the dispensary was strict allocation by list. On one occasion there were forty courses of an antibiotic, allocated to the children, the post-operative and a man who had been shot. A Mrs Lewandowska, aged forty-six, with pneumonia in the Zoo, was not on the list. Her fourteen-year-old daughter, who had been stealing food from half the district to keep her alive, came to the hospital door at night and stood without knocking. Catalina did not let her in. In her own account Pawel, who kept the stores, took one course of the antibiotic to the girl at three in the morning and asked to be entered in the ledger as part of the number. At a hearing in a chapel Catalina said that her rule was wrong and that she and Pawel had been together for eight months, and the room answered that everyone knew. Mrs Lewandowska lived. Alisia's account differs on one point: she says that Catalina came to the Zoo and looked at her mother. Catalina is not a doctor, and does not like to be called one in front of a patient. Diana found her at Brodno at forty, with a ledger in a green exercise book that set beside each stock count the number of people who would not receive the drug, which by her rule was nine a week. She contributed clinical notes to Protocol 003: of eighty-one exposed persons she treated, three did not become compliant, and each had been doing something for another person on the first day.
DATA.appears: Chapter 7: The Musician (named in Diana's diary of 17 November 2034); Chapter 8: The Medic (Alex's visit to Kraków, Diana's diary of 11 October 2034, and her recording); Chapter 9: The Dendron (Protocol 003), clinical notes, and Alex's closing note with her added sentence; Chapter 13: The Youngest (in Alisia's recording); Chapter 14: The Mouse (named once in Diana's diary of 4 November 2034)
DATA.reliability: C (5). Her earlier career, the ledger and the hearing are in Diana's diary and her own recording and agree with Protocol 003. Her age is 40 in Diana's diary of October 2034 and 41 in February 2036. Alisia's account differs from hers on whether she came to the Zoo.

DATA.name: Magda Wiśniewska
DATA.summary: The Listener. Transcribed the Palace loudspeaker.
DATA.entry: Magda Wiśniewska listens. She made the written transcript of the Palace loudspeaker broadcasts, morning and evening, and the archivist used her words unaltered. The four-second pause in the broadcast is on her page. Her transcript is the only record of the voice that a resident of Block C, Wiktor Szeliga, heard twice a day. She is called the Listener, a name she dislikes. Diana sat with her through the night of 21 to 22 September 2034 at OP-Rynek, in a long loft above the pharmacy with a sloping ceiling, a table of five radios, a lamp with a green shade and a notebook ruled in six columns. She was sixteen, thin and watchful, in a boy's anorak, and she asked at the door whether Diana wanted tea before she decided whether she was welcome. At the hourly check-in of the five Russian posts she said that the third was lying, and that a man telling the truth takes his breath after he starts to speak. She judged the Polish woman's voice on the northern recording to be a person asked to sound like a recording. Her transcripts are also the source of the words in Interlude III and Interlude VI, and her intercepts of the Russian net are rated 0.7 in Protocol 005. At eleven, in Mokotów, she gave the officers billeted in her house eleven names in return for chocolate and a pass, and four were taken to Szucha. She keeps the list. Alex met her in Lublin in March 2036, when she was eighteen.
DATA.appears: Interlude I: Wiktor Szeliga, Block C (transcript); Interlude III: Major Budanov, Aleja Szucha (transcript); Chapter 10: The Listener (Alex's visit, Diana's diary of 22 September 2034, and her recording); Chapter 11: The Orphan (Diana's diary of 30 November 2034 and Zoysa's recording); Chapter 14: The Mouse (a remark on Nikita); Interlude VI: Wiktor Szeliga, Shelter 9 (transcript); Chapter 15: The Aftermath (Protocol 005), source table
DATA.reliability: C (7). Her role as transcriber is stated in three interludes and Protocol 005. Her work at Rynek, her age (16 in September 2034, 18 in March 2036) and the list of eleven names are in Diana's diary, Alex's account and her own recording, and agree. Her truthfulness is itself in question in the chapter.

DATA.name: Zoysa Zieliński
DATA.summary: Aged 17 at the first account and 19 later. Captain at the Dęblin air academy.
DATA.entry: Zoysa was seventeen when she stood in the corner of Marek's kitchen on a Thursday, boots tucked under her, back against the wall, with the bearing of a girl taught to stand to attention before she could read. When the story ended she stood, said "Thank you, Pan Marek", and left without her coat. Later, aged nineteen, she received the archivist at the air academy at Dęblin, precisely at ten to the hour, in an office with a map on one wall. She was reported to be the youngest officer of her rank in the Polish army, and wore the rank as a thing issued rather than chosen. The academy had four hundred and six students, aged fourteen to thirty-one, eleven aircraft that fly and nineteen that do not. They keep the nineteen because they teach more. During one period she was absent two nights; Goya said she was on patrol, but the roster showed no entry. Her mother was killed on the first night of the invasion, when Zoysa was eleven. Her father, Colonel Andrzej Zieliński, was reported killed holding a bridge on the Bug when she was thirteen. She came to the Zone at fifteen and asked for the Kosciuszko Group, and Goya took her to the range and found that she could shoot. In November 2034 Magda told her that a man with her father's name and the rank of colonel had been heard on the Szucha net. On 2 December she crossed the river alone, without her coat, to a flat in Śródmieście, and found him alive and working for the occupiers. She did not shoot him. She made him her agent, and for seven months he gave the Brigade intelligence. She told Goya after the third month, and he did not speak to her for four days. She keeps a pad headed Order, a list of things in their place that includes the words Father, alive. In 2036 she visits her father in a flat in Lublin on Sundays.

DATA.name: Alisia Lewandowska
DATA.summary: Thief. Aged 14 when she stole to keep her mother alive, 16 when the archivist met her.
DATA.entry: Alisia Lewandowska was fourteen when she stole food from half the district to keep her mother alive. The mother, Mrs Lewandowska, was forty-six and had pneumonia in the Zoo. When Alex met her in Warsaw in March 2036 she was sixteen, small and quick, in a sweatshirt and a lanyard, and within a minute she had taken his pen from the table. She gave it back. A girl of about fourteen in a too-large grey anorak was seen entering the keeper's house at the Zoo by a side window with no catch. She took half a loaf, a bag of flour and a grey blanket in eleven seconds. Diana, who watched from the porch on 26 October 2034, knew her as Alisia and did not intervene. Nikita, aged six, laid a hand flat on the girl's wrist, and Alisia put back the bread and flour and left by the front door. She grew up at Hel, where her father, a fisherman, was lost in the first flood on the coast when she was nine. She stole from the age of five and by twelve was the best thief in the district. Her mother recovered, and now makes jam in Gdynia. On the morning after the keeper's house she went to the Brigade and confessed, and at fifteen she became its supply coordinator and kept its ledger. In 2036 she is the youngest investigator on a team of eleven at an anti-corruption foundation in Warsaw, and has twice visited Nikita in Wrocław.

DATA.name: Anna
DATA.summary: Elder of the two children at the keeper's house, aged about 13.
DATA.entry: Anna is perhaps thirteen. She and Nikita live in the keeper's house at the south end of the Zoo, in the old reptile garden, a small brick house with a pitched roof and a tin chimney, now belonging to Pan and Pani Wróbel, who took in both children. Diana visited the house on 26 October 2034 with a message from Catalina, and waited on the porch while Anna read in the back room. A girl came in at a side window and took bread, flour and a blanket. Nikita laid a hand on her wrist, and the goods were returned. By February 2036 Anna is fifteen, tall, with a long plait, and she and Nikita live in a flat in Wrocław, on the second floor of a block near the river. She has been in charge of Nikita since she was thirteen. The day after their parents were taken she found Nikita in a cupboard, carried her down the stairs on her back and took her into the sewers, where they stayed three weeks. Nikita calls her Little Bird. She keeps the rules of the flat: the kitchen door half open, a rubber washer on the tap, a clock that does not tick. Nikita made it a condition of Alex's visit that Anna be present. A fifth tap, five quick, was Diana's own, and Nikita has not asked for it since. Fritha says that Anna would know whether Nikita still has the print she was given.
