DATA.name: Nikita Sokołowski
DATA.summary: Aged 6. Does not speak. Hears what instruments do not.
DATA.entry: Nikita was six in 2034, when Diana knew her, and eight in 2036. She does not speak. She is frightened of a single knock, so visitors knock twice and wait. She and Diana built a language eleven items long, which is the only record of their exchanges. She has been hearing, throughout, what the instruments pick up and the adults do not. Diana filed her drawing under MAG_REF_400, the mark for the organism itself, and copied it in her own hand. It was the first time she took a symbol from a child. Nikita's own account, written for Alex in Wrocław in February 2036, says that she can speak and has decided not to. At six she heard five men on the stairs of their flat, whispered a warning to her father, and was put in a cupboard, and her parents did not return. She believed that the whisper had brought the men, and stopped making sound. Anna carried her into the sewers, where she heard patrols through the pipes and was the one who said stop. Diana first saw her at St Michael's, beside Fritha, on 9 August 2034. At the keeper's house she laid a hand flat on the wrist of a thief at the window. She hears a low note held under a cloth, and drew it as a circle with a wave in it and a cloth over the top. Diana judged her the most accurate instrument in the zone. The violin was the first sound that did not frighten her. The brief that Diana read on 28 December 2034 places her among the small proportion who resist the compound. In 2036 she paints in watercolours from a tin that Diana gave her, and cannot bear a ticking clock.
DATA.appears: Foreword (described, not named); Chapter 2: The Photographer (Diana's diary of 9 August 2034, and Fritha's recording); Chapter 13: The Youngest (Diana's diary of 26 October 2034, and Alisia's recording); Chapter 14: The Mouse (Alex's visit, Diana's diary of 4 November 2034, and her written account); Chapter 16: The Protocols (Diana's diary of 28 December 2034)
DATA.reliability: C (6). Diana's diaries of 9 August, 26 October and 4 November 2034, Alex's visit, her written account and Alisia's recording agree on her age (six in 2034, eight in 2036), her silence and her hearing. That she can speak and chooses not to rests on her own account alone (E).

facts.role: Child. Hears what the instruments do not
facts.distinguishing_trait: Does not speak. Frightened of a single knock.
facts.fate: Alive in 2036, living with Anna in Wrocław and painting in watercolours.

DATA.name: Artur Wójcik
DATA.summary: Boy of about 12 who works on the hand-built radio at Żerań.
DATA.entry: At Żerań Diana found a hand-built radio assembled from boards, scavenged parts and hand-wound coils, mounted in a gutted instrument case, and a boy of about twelve working on its inside with a tool he had made himself. Artur reads what makes a machine stall. In Lucasz's account, Artur worked out within about a week that the engineer had a fault that only one person could fix, and went to the Zoo to tell Tanja. He took the key from Lucasz's belt for the lock-in, and on the pressure-fall night he ran the dock gauge reading to Diana. Lucasz places the lock-in on a Thursday in late October. Goya stood at the door and Lucasz was kept in the control room for seven hours, while Tanja played on the step outside. Diana knew of it and neither took part nor stopped it. In her field note at Żerań an unnamed boy, probably Artur, tells her that Lucasz does not sleep but switches off like a lamp and then switches on. The manuscript gives the boy's age as about twelve at the arrival on 1 June 2034 and gives no surname.
DATA.appears: Diary 001: The Arrival (an unnamed boy of about twelve at the radio); Chapter 4: The Engineer (Diana's field note, where the boy is unnamed, and Lucasz's recording, which names Artur); Interlude: The Second Flood (Diana's note on the pressure fall)
DATA.reliability: E (4). Named in two passages (Chapter 4, Lucasz's recording; Interlude: The Second Flood). The boy at the radio in Diary 001 and in Chapter 4 is unnamed and is identified by role. The surname Wójcik, the age of 11 and the work on drones are in the project brief only (U).

facts.role: Builds and repairs the radio at Żerań
facts.distinguishing_trait: Reads what makes a machine stall. Makes his own tools.

DATA.name: Pawel
DATA.summary: Former banker, aged 35. Keeps the stores. Will not carry a weapon.
DATA.entry: Pawel was a banker, thirty-five. He was in Warsaw because his father was in a nursing home in Praga and could not be moved, and when the water came he would not leave him. He stayed until the old man died, then stayed because he did not know where else to go. He keeps the stores and counts. He will not carry a weapon and that is the whole of his reputation. Men who had been at Mariupol called him a coward. Catalina did not, and says of him that he decided at some cost what he will not do. In the ward at Brodno, in Diana's diary of 11 October 2034, Goya told him to count the blood on the floor, and he did. His ears went red and his pencil stopped, then began again. Catalina's recording supplies the rest. They were together for eight months before it was known. He took one course of antibiotics from the dispensary at three in the morning, with the key she had left on a hook, and put it in the hand of Alisia Lewandowska at the Zoo for her mother, who was not on the list. He told Catalina in the morning and said she could put him in the number. At the hearing in the chapel she said the rule was wrong and that they were together, and the room answered that it already knew. In February 2036 they are still together in Kraków, where he does the accounts for her organisation. Diana put him in his mid-thirties in 2034. Alex, meeting him in Kraków, describes a thin man in his mid-forties in a good coat that has lost some of its edge.
DATA.appears: Chapter 8: The Medic (Diana's diary of 11 October 2034 at OP-Brodno; Catalina's recording; Alex's closing scene in Kraków, February 2036); Chapter 13: The Youngest (Alisia's recording)
DATA.reliability: C (4). Diana's diary, Catalina's recording, Alex's scene in Kraków and Alisia's recording agree on the banker, the stores and the refusal to carry a weapon. The ages given (35 by Catalina, mid-thirties by Diana, mid-forties by Alex in 2036) do not fit one another (U).

facts.role: Keeps the stores. Former banker
facts.distinguishing_trait: Will not carry a weapon.
facts.fate: Alive in 2036, doing the accounts for Catalina's organisation in Kraków.

DATA.name: Marek Olszewski
DATA.summary: Elder of the community. Tells stories on Thursdays.
DATA.entry: Marek and Rosa are the two old people of the Zone, who passed through earlier wars as children and as parents. They keep a third-floor flat in Białołęka that stayed above the water. On Thursdays Marek tells stories at the kitchen table to whoever comes, Rosa makes tea and the children sit under the table, which is the warm place. Diana counted eleven present at one telling, on 30 November 2034, and chose not to record it, because some things are for being in the room. That night he told of a Home Army captain in the sewers under Śródmieście in August 1944, who kept a note offering terms in his coat for four days and never burned it. Marek said he had never decided what to think. Zoysa, in the corner by the stove, thanked him formally and left without her coat. In Protocol 005 he says, over tea with the children under the table, that the people of 1944 were killed by those who watched as well as by the Germans, and that he had waited ninety years for someone to say it aloud. Zoysa quotes his view that it does not matter whether the man in a story was a hero, only that the story was told.
DATA.appears: Chapter 5: The Pilgrim (Janek's testimony); Chapter 11: The Orphan (Diana's diary of 30 November 2034; Zoysa's recording); Chapter 15: The Aftermath (Protocol 005), section 6, The Parallel
DATA.reliability: C (4). Janek's testimony, Diana's diary, Zoysa's recording and Protocol 005 agree on the flat and the Thursday tellings. His age is not given; he is a child in August 1944 and says he has waited ninety years.

facts.age: About 90. A child in the city in August 1944
facts.role: Elder. Tells stories on Thursdays
facts.distinguishing_trait: Tells stories at the kitchen table, with the children under it.

DATA.name: Rosa Olszewska
DATA.summary: Elder who gave Janek a room.
DATA.entry: Rosa shares the third-floor flat in Białołęka with Marek. In September she offered Janek the empty back room, saying it had been empty since the winter. She makes tea at Marek's Thursday tellings. Janek had said he was only passing through, and she answered that he had been passing through for eleven years. He took the room in October and lived in it through the second winter. Diana, who had come with Marek to carry a table, asked him whether he could not have the room or did not think he was allowed. At the telling of 30 November 2034 Rosa puts her hand on Marek's sleeve in the silence after the story. A Pani Olszewska, probably Rosa, speaks gently at the chapel hearing where Alisia Lewandowska confesses her thefts, and tells her that if she knows where everything is, she can tell them.
DATA.appears: Chapter 5: The Pilgrim (Janek's testimony); Chapter 11: The Orphan (Diana's diary of 30 November 2034); Chapter 13: The Youngest (Alisia's recording; Pani Olszewska, probably Rosa)
DATA.reliability: C (3). Janek's testimony and Diana's diary name her directly. The Pani Olszewska of Alisia's recording is given no first name (E).

facts.role: Elder
facts.distinguishing_trait: Makes the tea at Marek's tellings. Gave Janek a room.

DATA.name: The Runners
DATA.summary: Couriers, mostly children. Also called the Ducks.
DATA.entry: The Runners are mostly children who carry messages when the Russians jam the air, going where a boat would be seen and a man would be shot. Goya says they are called the Ducks, "whatever they're calling them this year". They keep waypoints in the forest and use a winter route recorded in the Protocol 001 tables. A Runner of about thirteen was brought to the ward at Brodno by Goya with a bullet through the forearm and behaved as if it were a bee sting. Goya knows where each Runner in the wetlands is at any hour. A Runner stood at the church door when Diana first heard of Fritha and would not go in. A Runner first reported the hum of the Dendron to Diana, who did not at first believe her. On the night of the second flood Goya put twenty-three Runners out in four boats, the youngest nine, and counted twenty-three back. Iga, a Runner aged 23, was one of three lost at the Docks that night, having gone back for a boat. Runners brought the first reports of the third flood, including gunboats entering the canal at 04:00. A girl of about fifteen, Oliwia, carried Diana's last item in her boot for fourteen months and got out.
DATA.appears: Chapter 1: The Blasphemer (Goya's recording; Diana's note); Chapter 2: The Photographer; Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001); Interlude: The Second Flood; Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), section 6.1; Chapter 8: The Medic; Chapter 9: The Dendron (Protocol 003), section 3.1; Chapter 15: The Aftermath (Protocol 005); Chapter 16: The Protocols
DATA.reliability: C (10). Present from Goya's first recording to the last chapter, and the accounts agree that they carry messages. Individual Runners named: Iga (23) and Oliwia (about 15).

facts.role: Couriers
facts.distinguishing_trait: Mostly children. Carry messages when the air is jammed.

DATA.name: Alex, the archivist
DATA.summary: Journalist who assembled the Protocols after the war.
DATA.entry: Alex is the narrator of the archive. He is a journalist, sent into the Zone by the Guardian for a week. A postcard led him to a farm east of Warsaw, where Diana Antonoff had left her notebooks, binders, tapes and photographs with a note asking him to make them public. He then visited the speakers in Gdańsk, Berlin, Przemyśl, Wrocław, Kraków, Lublin, Dęblin and Warsaw (datelines November 2035 to March 2036) and set the book in Diana's order. The five Protocols and the notes against each transcript are hers. Where he writes a reconstruction he puts it in italics and brackets, names the source of each passage, and says what he supplied himself. He met Diana once, for half an hour, at a farm in the grey zone in the last days before she went in. In each interlude he states that he never met the subject, builds one day in the subject's voice from the surviving papers, and asks that the invented man not be taken for a witness.
DATA.appears: Foreword; Prologue: The Barn; the framing passages of Chapters 1 to 16; the reconstructions in Interlude I: Wiktor Szeliga, Block C, Interlude II: Sasha Lebedev, Observation Post R0, Interlude III: Major Budanov, Aleja Szucha, Interlude IV: The Voice, Studio Two, Interlude V: Account Lead, Cohort Review, and Interlude VI: Wiktor Szeliga, Shelter 9
DATA.reliability: C (6). Self-description in the Foreword, the Prologue and the prefaces to Interludes I to VI. The surname Kovalchuk comes from the older profile. The manuscript has one transcription credit to an A. Kovalchuk, on Nikita's written account in Chapter 14, and nothing there says that this is Alex (U).

facts.role: Journalist. Assembled the archive
facts.distinguishing_trait: Marks his reconstructions in italics and brackets, and names the source of each passage.

Interlude II: Sasha Lebedev, Observation Post R0
Interlude III: Major Budanov, Aleja Szucha
Interlude IV: The Voice, Studio Two

DATA.name: Wiktor Szeliga
DATA.summary: Resident of Block C. Left no testimony.
DATA.entry: Wiktor Szeliga gave no testimony and kept no diary. His traces are a pencil ration ledger kept by the block warden, Magda Wiśniewska's transcript of the Palace loudspeaker, nine minutes of Diana's tape and a neighbour's account given in Lublin after the war. On the fifteenth he crossed the Vistula. The ledger records one adult male, ambulant, and one female child, nine, ambulant. A line for a non-ambulant person is ruled through, with no entry beside it. The neighbour said someone had gone up on the Thursday, that it was very quiet, that the room had been tidied and the bed made. He is a man who counts stairs. The child is Marta, his sister's daughter, who came to him in June and has not spoken since the sixth day. Interlude VI, set on 14 June 2035, finds the two of them in Shelter 9, a former sports hall on the left bank, in beds 118 and 117. The ledger lists him as an orderly and has him on the potato detail for 302 mornings of 304. A gold ring on a shoelace was found in a cloakroom coat. On the last night the ledger records him awake and sitting up, and a second hand adds "Leave him". The following page is torn out, and the archivist does not know what became of him. Marta, grown, is a nurse in Gdańsk, and the only witness to anything he said.
DATA.appears: Interlude I: Wiktor Szeliga, Block C; Interlude VI: Wiktor Szeliga, Shelter 9
DATA.reliability: E (10). Interlude I draws on four sources (a ledger, a transcript, Diana's tape, a neighbour); Interlude VI on a Shelter 9 ledger, a rota, a drawing, a ring, a leaflet and an interview with the grown Marta. None is his own, and the archivist states that each is a reconstruction.

facts.role: Resident of Block C. Later an orderly at Shelter 9
facts.distinguishing_trait: Counts stairs. A man of order.
facts.fate: Unknown. The ledger page after his last night is torn out.

facts.first_appearance_t: Interlude I: Wiktor Szeliga, Block C

DATA.name: Sasha Lebedev
DATA.summary: Russian operator at Observation Post R0. Relieved on 11 October.
DATA.entry: Sasha Lebedev left no account. The archive holds eleven photocopied rota sheets, the post log in a green hardback notebook with a red spine, forty-four text messages from his mother recovered from a handset left in a drawer, a chocolate-bar wrapper and a receipt. On R0 he reads the sixth-day rota aloud to six field commanders, who answer "Received" and a number. He says "B" in place of the name of the authorising officer and keeps the same voice at the same speed throughout. He was relieved on 11 October. The log passes to a blocky, heavy hand. On the first page of that hand is the old instruction, "Do not add anything. Do not leave anything out. Do not pause", and under it in pencil, in another hand, "He paused." Protocol 002, section 7.3, gives him as a contracted operator and not a regular officer, aged 23 (E); in the reconstruction he gives the same age, from his mother's messages. Survivors call him the Watcher, the boy on the radio (section 11.1). His room is four metres by three, with a steel shutter raised twenty centimetres. Through that strip he sees an eleven-storey block opposite whose lower four floors are covered by the green growth, and a man's blue shirt on a sixth-floor balcony that has not moved in ninety-four days. The reconstructed day is 4 October. On 2 October the 06:00 transmission stops for four minutes and four seconds, and the log of the third records an equipment fault; the archivist says he does not know what he did in that time. A receipt for milk, sugar and a lighter, from a petrol station on the Radzymin road, is dated that afternoon. In Chapter 10, Magda Wiśniewska says she knew his voice from the net, and took the gap of 2 October for a message.
DATA.appears: Interlude II: Sasha Lebedev, Observation Post R0; Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), sections 7.3, 8 and 11.1; Chapter 10: The Listener (Magda Wiśniewska's account of his voice)
DATA.reliability: E (4). Interlude II is a reconstruction from documents, with interviews with men who did the same work used with stated caution. Protocol 002 gives his age and the gap of 2 October (U, one intercept). In Chapter 10 Magda says she cannot be certain it was the same voice.

facts.age: 23 (E); in the reconstruction he gives the same age
facts.role: Contracted operator at Observation Post R0
facts.distinguishing_trait: Reads the rota in the same voice at the same speed.
facts.fate: Relieved on 11 October 2034. Nothing further is recorded.
facts.own_protocol_t: Interlude II: Sasha Lebedev, Observation Post R0
facts.first_appearance_t: Interlude II: Sasha Lebedev, Observation Post R0

DATA.name: Colonel Viktor Nikolaevich Sorokin
DATA.summary: Commanding officer of the occupying force. Based at the Citadel.
DATA.entry: Aged approximately 55 (E). His record, as far as it is known, is that of a professional: no excesses are attributed to him or to his staff in his name. He does not appear to hate the city. He appears to have orders and the competence to carry them out. It is reported that he reads. A source who delivered food to his office in July saw a clear desk with a single paperback and a glass of water. The title was not seen. Protocol 002 gives him first of three men, named in full with patronymic as they appear on the one set of orders recovered. It is Major Budanov's name, and not the colonel's, that appears on the orders. Survivors call the colonel the Iron One.
DATA.appears: Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), sections 7.1 and 11.1
DATA.reliability: E (2). Section 7.1 gives his age and character from sources who did not meet him. Section 11.1 gives the survivors' name for him. Rank, name and patronymic come from one set of recovered orders.

facts.role: Commanding officer of the occupying force
facts.distinguishing_trait: Reads. Keeps a clear desk with a single paperback and a glass of water.

DATA.name: Major Budanov
DATA.summary: Head of screening and intelligence, Aleja Szucha. His office issues the rota. Referred to as "B".
DATA.entry: Major Budanov's office issues the sixth-day rota at 06:00. It lists the day's movements by block, time, crew, task, duration, authorising officer and status. Each task is authorised "B". Operators read the order without saying the name. Protocol 002, section 7.2, gives his full name as Major Alexei Dmitrievich Budanov, aged approximately 44 (E), operating from Szucha. He is thorough, courteous to those brought in, and said to speak good Polish with an accent that recalls Kraków (C, two returned persons). He signs the letter D with a flourish. Survivors call him the Spaniel, for the way he hunts. Interlude III reconstructs one day at Aleja Szucha from a 212-page procedures binder, an appointments diary, a canteen card, a desk inventory and about three hundred of 4,100 numbered screening forms, found in eleven boxes in a basement in Praga. The archivist never met him and says the order of the day is his own. Each form ends in one of four words, and the last two are never explained on any form. One form records an interpreter who did not take the sweet offered at the fourth step, and Budanov notes in the margin that he is curious about her. Those who served under him would say only that he was always polite.
DATA.appears: Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), sections 7.2, 11.1 and 11.2; Interlude II: Sasha Lebedev, Observation Post R0; Interlude III: Major Budanov, Aleja Szucha
DATA.reliability: E (3). Protocol 002 gives him from a recovered set of orders and from two returned persons. Interlude II gives the rota. Interlude III is a reconstruction in which the archivist states that the order of the day is his own; the binder, diary, forms and photographed desk are the record.

facts.role: Head of screening and intelligence, Aleja Szucha
facts.distinguishing_trait: Thorough and courteous. Signs the letter D with a flourish.
facts.own_protocol_t: Interlude III: Major Budanov, Aleja Szucha
facts.first_appearance_t: Interlude II: Sasha Lebedev, Observation Post R0

apps.t: Interlude II: Sasha Lebedev, Observation Post R0
Interlude III: Major Budanov, Aleja Szucha

DATA.name: Captain Isaev
DATA.summary: Officer of the day at the Poniatowski Bridge checkpoint, aged 31.
DATA.entry: Captain Isaev is thirty-one and sweats a little. He reports to Major Budanov at 08:40. He declines tea once, then accepts it. On the night in question there were 212 crossings. Of these, 190 were assessed on the bridge at Stage 2 or 3 and passed to the reception hall on the left bank. Twenty-two did not pass. He was asked what became of them and told the officer. He is the officer of the day at the checkpoint on the Poniatowski Bridge. Budanov receives him after reading fourteen overnight reports, each twice, once for fact and once for what is left out. The answer about the twenty-two is not given, and Isaev appears nowhere else in the manuscript. The manuscript gives no first name.
DATA.appears: Interlude III: Major Budanov, Aleja Szucha
DATA.reliability: E (1). One passage, inside a day that the archivist says he reconstructed and ordered himself. The passage carries no source tag, so the figures may be the archivist's (U).

facts.role: Officer of the day, Poniatowski Bridge checkpoint
facts.distinguishing_trait: Sweats a little. Declines tea once, then accepts it.

DATA.name: Mrs Lewandowska
DATA.summary: Alisia's mother, aged 46, ill with pneumonia in the Zoo.
DATA.entry: Mrs Lewandowska had pneumonia and was not on Catalina's antibiotic list. Her daughter stole food from half the district to keep her alive. She was forty-six, and lay in a shed at the Zoo in the autumn of 2034. Catalina's rule left nine people a week untreated, and the last forty courses of an antibiotic had been allocated without her. Alisia came to the hospital door at night and stood there without knocking. Pawel took one course from the dispensary and put it in Alisia's hand. Mrs Lewandowska lived. In March 2036 Alisia says she is in Gdynia and makes jam. Diana's note on Catalina's transcript names her as the ninth, the number in the ledger that was never a count. Before the war the family lived at Hel, where her husband, a fisherman, drowned after taking a neighbour off a roof in the first flood. Alisia says his boat, the Marzena, was named for her mother.
DATA.appears: Chapter 8: The Medic (Catalina's recording; Diana's note on the transcript); Chapter 13: The Youngest (Alisia's recording)
DATA.reliability: C (3). Catalina's recording, Diana's note on it and Alisia's recording agree on the pneumonia, the list and the recovery. Her first name is not given.

facts.role: Alisia's mother
facts.distinguishing_trait: Ill with pneumonia, and not on Catalina's list.
facts.fate: Lived. Makes jam in Gdynia in 2036.

DATA.name: Pan and Pani Wróbel
DATA.summary: Elderly couple who took in Anna and Nikita.
DATA.entry: Pan and Pani Wróbel are an elderly couple who live in the keeper's house at the south end of the Zoo and have taken in two children, Anna and Nikita. The house is a small brick building inside the old reptile garden, with a pitched roof and a tin chimney. One side window has no catch. On the afternoon of 26 October 2034 Pani Wróbel was out at the cistern, Pan Wróbel was asleep in a chair and Anna was reading in the back room, when Alisia Lewandowska took a half loaf, a bag of flour and a folded grey blanket from the shelf by the stove. Nikita laid a hand on her wrist, and Alisia put everything back. A visitor is told to knock twice and wait, because Nikita is frightened of a single knock. The house is also the setting of Diana's diary of 4 November 2034 in Chapter 14, which does not name the couple.
DATA.appears: Chapter 13: The Youngest (Diana's diary of 26 October 2034; Alisia's recording)
DATA.reliability: E (2). Named in two passages of one chapter, both concerned with the theft. No first names are given.

facts.role: Keep the keeper's house at the Zoo
facts.distinguishing_trait: Took in two children, Anna and Nikita.

DATA.name: Mrs Kaczmarek
DATA.summary: Old woman at the Zoo who leaves milk for the Dendron each morning and has stayed at stage 1 for three months.
DATA.entry: Mrs Kaczmarek is an old woman at the Zoo. Her first name and her age are not given. She believes that the Dendron has been sent to teach people patience. Every morning at seven she leaves a saucer of milk at the foot of the largest mass. Diana records her in the notes to file of Protocol 003 as a person at stage 1 who has not passed to stage 2, and who has been at stage 1 for three months. Diana asked Catalina Chmielewska how that was possible. Catalina answered that the saucer is for someone else. Diana does not say what Catalina meant. In her diary of 28 December 2034, after she has read the brief, Diana writes of the woman at the Zoo who leaves milk for the organism and repeats the reason. She counts her among the forty thousand in the brief, as a datum, and does not give her name. Section 8 of Protocol 003 reports that the three persons who did not become compliant were each doing something for someone else on the first day. The manuscript does not connect Mrs Kaczmarek to them. It records no other speech or action by her and does not follow her beyond these two passages.
DATA.appears: Chapter 9: The Dendron (Protocol 003), section 11.2; Chapter 16: The Protocols (Diana's diary of 28 December 2034, where she is not named)
DATA.reliability: E (2). Both passages are Diana's. Her belief about the Dendron and the three months are reported by Diana and not otherwise witnessed. No other character mentions her.

facts.role: Resident of the Zoo
facts.distinguishing_trait: Leaves a saucer of milk for the Dendron every morning at seven.
facts.fate: At stage 1 for three months. Not followed further.

DATA.name: Dendron
DATA.summary: An organism of great age, recovered from permafrost, that spreads with floodwater and sedates those who stay near it.
DATA.entry: The Dendron is the organism that spread through the Warsaw corridor with the flood. The name is a survivor's name. Dendron is Greek for tree, and the organism is not a tree. It is reported to be of great age, recovered from permafrost in northern Siberia before the war, studied in Soviet laboratories for decades and made available for military use in the last years before the invasion. A Russian scientist who fled describes it as the first thing that was alive before anyone decided what alive meant. It climbs walls, pipes, railings and the iron of tram wires, and prefers damp, shade and the dark inside things. It clogs drains and sewers, so that the water rises and the organism grows in the new water. It makes a sustained tone at approximately 180 Hz with a slow beat of about six seconds, loudest at night and over still air. Those exposed to the compound do not appear to hear it. It emits a compound that is not a toxin and does not kill. It sedates. The effect is recorded in four stages, from unusual calm at stage 1 to obedience to any instruction at stage 4. In winter the visible growth retreats. Below 8 degrees Celsius the organism closes, and exposure is much less dangerous. Exposure is reduced by distance, by cold, by keeping upwind, and by filtration. It does not grow on the bricks of the Żerań power station, and no reason is known. The stem is the width of a finger and the colour of wet slate, and it has no leaves. Paired structures along it, about nine centimetres apart, show grey-white when open above 8 degrees Celsius. At the Żerań cooling channel a mature mass lowered the water level by 11 centimetres in nine days. In summer it is dense and hides. Wind is the main way exposure travels in the open, and the Filtry water station supplies the only water in the corridor reliably free of the compound. Catalina Chmielewska had treated eighty-one persons with documented exposure when the Protocol was compiled, and three of them did not become compliant. At the Zoo an old woman, Mrs Kaczmarek, leaves milk at the foot of the largest mass each morning at seven and has stayed at stage 1 for three months. The Russian word for what it does, mir, is also the word for peace. A hum with a six second beat is heard in Interlude IV and Interlude VI, and a sound of 180 hertz with the same beat is played beneath the interview table in Interlude III. The manuscript does not say that these are the Dendron's tone.
DATA.appears: Foreword, where the Protocols are said to hold a pharmacology of it. Prologue: The Barn, as rumour. Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), sections 9 and 12.4. Chapter 9: The Dendron (Protocol 003), in full. Chapter 12: The Codex (Protocol 004), section 4.3, where it receives its mark. Chapter 15: The Aftermath (Protocol 005), section 7, where the organism is described as supplied from the permafrost. Chapter 16: The Protocols, Diana's diary of 28 December 2034. Its sound, without the name, in Interlude: The Second Flood.
DATA.reliability: C (7 passages: the Foreword, the Prologue and Chapters 3, 9, 12, 15 and 16). The least reliable of the Protocols, by its own account: the organism has not been clinically studied. Spread: C, several sources. Sound: C, recorded on eleven nights by Diana. Distance beyond about 40 metres: E. Vinegar mask, reduction by perhaps half: E, one source. Origin in Siberian permafrost: E, the scientist, and the brief as Diana reports it in Protocol 005.

facts.holder: The programme. Supplied by the Russian state
facts.origin: Recovered from permafrost in northern Siberia and studied in Soviet laboratories
facts.function: Sedates those exposed to its compound, in four stages
facts.last_seen: Throughout the corridor, retreating in the cold of December 2034

images.alt: Silhouetted hands press against a window laced with dark, vine-like tendrils. Beyond the glass, tower blocks stand in fog.

DATA.name: Dendron Dust
DATA.summary: A pale powder scraped from the surface of mature Dendron growth.
DATA.entry: The surface of a mature mass of the Dendron carries a pale powder in dry conditions. It can be scraped off. It is known in the corridor as Dendron Dust. In the dry months of summer the wind lifts it from the surface and carries it some distance, and it is then more widely spread than in any other season. Wet, it does not keep. Where it falls into standing water it dissolves, and the water that takes it is afterwards, in its effect, no different from water that carries the compound. Raw, it carries a trace of the compound, and breathed in on the wind it dulls as the water does. Prepared by those who gather it, scraped, dried and cut, and taken in the amounts used, it has the opposite effect. It is gathered in the cold months, when the organism is slow, and not in summer. Taken, the dust acts as a psychedelic. Members of the resistance use it in rituals.
DATA.appears: Chapter 9: The Dendron (Protocol 003), section 7, Dendron Dust. Chapter 12: The Codex (Protocol 004), section 4.3, where the secondary mark for the Dust is given.
DATA.reliability: C (1 substantive passage, Protocol 003 section 7, with a second mention in Protocol 004 section 4.3). The spread by wind and the dissolving in water are graded C by the Protocol, two sources, not confirmed clinically. The psychedelic use and the rituals rest on that passage alone, reported to Diana and not attended by her: E.

facts.holder: Those who gather it, and members of the resistance
facts.origin: Scraped from the surface of mature Dendron masses
facts.function: Prepared and taken, a psychedelic used in rituals. Raw, it dulls as the compound does

DATA.name: The Protocols (Diana's bequest)
DATA.summary: The collected papers and recordings Diana left, from which the archive is assembled.
DATA.entry: The archivist found the body of Diana's work beneath a canvas covering: three binders, a box of cassette tapes and some memory cards, a canvas roll of photographs and, laid across her notebooks where he would find it first, a manila folder with his name on it in her handwriting. The handwriting is deliberate, slanted forward, with the name underlined twice. Binder one is reproduced as found at the head of the relevant Protocols. Binder two holds annexes, among them Annex A, a list of forty-one streets given with both their present and their pre-1944 names, which the survivors use. The tapes carry the recorded testimonies. The four notebooks were wrapped separately in oilcloth and laid on top. The single sheet in the folder tells Alex to make the Protocols public. Diana counts forty cassettes by 2 September 2034. The Foreword speaks of five Protocols. Chapters 3, 6, 9, 12 and 15 each open with one, marked as binder one and reproduced as found, and Protocol 004 records that binder one holds Protocols 001 to 003 and itself. Binder two holds the crate label, a page giving the name of the programme, the initial of the Russian scientist and the brief in full. The binder of Budanov's procedures in Interlude III is a different object. Alex says that Protocol 005 reached him by another route, in a pouch kept in a Runner's boot for fourteen months.
DATA.appears: Foreword, the discovery and the contents. Interlude: The Second Flood, Diana's diaries of 28 August and 2 September 2034, for the notebooks, cassettes and memory cards. Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), section 10, for Annex A. Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), the binder one heading. Chapter 9: The Dendron (Protocol 003), section 10, for the second binder. Chapter 12: The Codex (Protocol 004), sections 2 and 3.1. Chapter 15: The Aftermath (Protocol 005), section 7 and Alex's closing note. Chapter 16: The Protocols, Diana's diary of 30 December 2034 and Alex's closing note.
DATA.reliability: C (8 passages: the Foreword, Interlude: The Second Flood and Chapters 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 and 16). The Foreword describes the bundle as found. Binder three is not described in any passage. The Foreword's count of five Protocols does not agree with Alex's account of how Protocol 005 arrived.

facts.function: The source of the archive: binders, tapes, notebooks and photographs
facts.last_seen: Beneath a canvas covering at a farm east of Warsaw, where Alex found it

DATA.name: Appendix: The Brief
DATA.summary: The document that names the programme behind the Dendron.
DATA.entry: The Brief is the document that Diana received on 28 December 2034, which Protocol 005 describes in part and which Alex reproduces in full in the appendix of the manuscript, from the second binder. It records Operation Neural Harvest, its origins, the parties that supplied the organism and the science, and its stated aim, population compliance optimisation, set down without comment. It is eleven pages, in Russian and in English, on the stationery of a research directorate, stamped, numbered and signed with initials. Diana does not copy the names of the Western partners, on the ground that a binder can be found. In the appendix each place where a partner name stood is marked withheld, and the initials of the signatories are not copied either. The brief is marked Restricted and copy 3 of 5, gives ethical review as not applicable, and is distributed to the Directorate, the Operator and three partner establishments. The brief describes the survivors, about forty thousand, as a test cohort, the flood as a delivery system, the stages of the organism's effect as behavioural endpoints, and stage 4 as the target state. It gives the city's qualities as isolated, contained and non-attributable. It holds the results in a joint repository, to be shared with partners on completion of the cohort phase, sets a target of not less than 60 per cent of the cohort at stage 3 or above within 90 days of continuous exposure, and expects a small proportion of the population to show atypical resistance. Four annexes, A to D, are listed in it and are not reproduced. Diana reads it four times on 28 December 2034 and finds the tidiness of it the worst part. In Interlude V a brief of matching wording is on slide four of a deck. The manuscript does not say that it is the same document.
DATA.appears: Chapter 15: The Aftermath (Protocol 005), sections 2, 7 and 8. Chapter 16: The Protocols, Diana's diary of 28 December 2034. Chapter 9: The Dendron (Protocol 003), section 10, in Alex's note that the brief is reproduced in the second binder. Interlude V: Account Lead, Cohort Review, slide four, as a brief of matching wording. Appendix: The Brief, in full.
DATA.reliability: C (4 passages: Protocol 003 section 10, Protocol 005 sections 2 and 7, Diana's diary of 28 December 2034 and the appendix itself). The full text is Appendix: The Brief, reproduced by Alex from the second binder with the partners' names and the signatories' initials withheld. The four annexes are listed and not reproduced. Interlude V gives a brief of matching wording, not stated to be the same document: E.

facts.holder: Diana, in binder two. Reproduced by Alex
facts.origin: A Russian research directorate. Reached Diana through the Russian scientist
facts.function: Sets out Operation Neural Harvest

apps.t: Interlude V: Account Lead, Cohort Review

DATA.name: Janek's prayer book
DATA.summary: Taped prayer book, one of Janek's three possessions.
DATA.entry: Janek owns a coat, a pair of boots and a prayer book. The spine of the book has been taped many times, and the older layers of tape show yellow under the new. He let Diana hold it for about a minute, on the dock at Żerań on 19 August 2034. On another occasion he put it on the oilcloth between them, spine up, in the course of a conversation. The occasion was Alex's visit to Janek in Przemyśl in January 2036. Janek told him that Diana had held the book for about a minute, and that it was the first time anyone had held it who did not want it to be anything. Alex asked to photograph it, and Janek refused. Janek studied for the priesthood and left it to marry, and his wife died of cancer five years before the invasion. Goya, in Chapter 1, remembers him as a man who owned nothing in the world but a coat and a book.
DATA.appears: Chapter 1: The Blasphemer, in Goya's remark about Janek's coat and book. Chapter 5: The Pilgrim, in Diana's diary of 19 August 2034 and in Alex's visit to Janek in Przemyśl, January 2036.
DATA.reliability: C (3 passages: Chapter 1, and two in Chapter 5). The tape, the minute and the three possessions are in the diary. The later scene agrees on the tape and the minute.

facts.function: Prayer book. One of his three possessions
facts.last_seen: Przemyśl, January 2036, on the oilcloth between Janek and Alex

DATA.name: Fritha's prints
DATA.summary: Forty-one family photographs recovered from the flood.
DATA.entry: Forty-one prints were carried in her father's jacket, which Fritha found on a railing six days after the flood. They were dried on a radiator in a stairwell without power. The emulsion had lifted and her mother's face had shifted a little to the left. Her family had gone back for eleven albums in the forty minutes after the dam went, and the prints are what she took out of the water. She dried them in front of a stove made from a bucket. Her father was a photographer with a studio in Praga, and her mother worked in conservation at the National Museum. The forty-one began a larger collection. By 9 August 2034 Diana found several thousand photographs in rows on the altar steps of St Michael's in Praga, each weighted at the corners with a pebble or a spent cartridge and sorted by year.
DATA.appears: Chapter 2: The Photographer, in Fritha's recording of November 2035 and in Diana's diary of 9 August 2034. Chapter 15: The Aftermath (Protocol 005), section 6, where Diana notes that Fritha holds several thousand photographs.
DATA.reliability: C (3 passages). The forty-one prints rest on Fritha's own recording. The larger collection is in Diana's diary of 9 August 2034 and in Protocol 005 section 6.

facts.origin: Carried in her father's jacket, found on a railing six days after the flood
facts.function: Family photographs. The start of Fritha's collection
facts.last_seen: St Michael's, Praga, 9 August 2034, on the altar steps

DATA.name: Operation Neural Harvest
DATA.summary: The Russian research programme under which the surviving population of Warsaw was held as a test cohort.
DATA.entry: Neural Harvest is the name of a research programme described in an operational brief that Diana Antonoff received on 28 December, through the Russian scientist she calls a source in Protocol 003. The brief is eleven pages, in Russian and in English, on the stationery of a research directorate, stamped and numbered. Hers was copy 3 of 5. The brief treats the survivors of the Warsaw corridor, estimated at forty thousand, as a test cohort. It treats the flood as the delivery system. It records the effects of the organism as behavioural endpoints in four stages and names stage 4 as the target state. The brief names loss of containment as the principal risk to the programme, and loss of the measurement through the emergence of an organised population as the secondary risk. It considers both low. A small proportion of the cohort is expected to show atypical resistance. Such subjects are to be identified, monitored and recorded. They are not to be removed from the cohort unless they affect the integrity of the measurement. The target for the cohort phase is that not less than 60 per cent of the cohort is assessed at stage 3 or above within 90 days of the establishment of continuous exposure. The phase ends when the Directorate determines that the measurement is complete. Results are held in a joint repository and are to be shared with the partner establishments on completion of the cohort phase. The brief gives ethical review as not applicable and states no reason. The name comes from the observation section: a harvest is the gathering of what has grown. The brief is reproduced as Appendix: The Brief, with the names of the Western partners and the initials withheld. It lists four annexes: A, the organism; B, delivery; C, behavioural endpoints; and D, observation, cordon and data. They are in the binder and are not reproduced. The programme is described as joint, run by the Russian state and at least two Western states through their agencies, military research establishments and private biotechnology contractors. The Russians supplied the organism and the Western partners supplied the means of enhancing it, stabilising it in a water supply and optimising it. The brief gives the grounds for the choice of city as isolated, contained and non-attributable, with no external access and no prospect of relief. The scientist gave Diana the name on 30 October 2034, and she wrote it in the second binder, not in Protocol 003. She believes the cohort phase ended with the destruction of Żerań on 1 January 2035, and rates that belief 0.6. In Interlude V an account lead works on a contract called the Programme, whose name has two words, one suggesting the brain and one a verb for gathering a crop.
DATA.appears: Chapter 9: The Dendron (Protocol 003), section 10, where the scientist gives the programme a name that Diana writes only in the second binder. Chapter 15: The Aftermath (Protocol 005), sections 2, 7, 8 and 9. Chapter 16: The Protocols, Diana's diary of 28 December 2034. Interlude V: Account Lead, Cohort Review, as the Programme. Without the name, in the instruments it uses: Interlude II: Sasha Lebedev, Observation Post R0, and Interlude III: Major Budanov, Aleja Szucha. Appendix: The Brief, in full.
DATA.reliability: C (5 passages: Protocol 003 section 10, Protocol 005 sections 2 and 7, Diana's diary of 28 December 2034, Appendix: The Brief and Interlude V). The brief as a document: seen and read by Diana, C, rated 0.8 as source 7 in Protocol 005. Its route to her: the Russian scientist, E. Interlude V gives the name only by description. Appendix: The Brief states copy 3 of 5, the target of 60 per cent at stage 3 or above within 90 days, the entry that ethical review is not applicable, and the titles of annexes A to D, which are listed and not reproduced. An earlier figure of less than one per cent and an earlier reasoning on elimination are not in the manuscript and are replaced in the Entry by the brief's own wording.

facts.period: Before the invasion to 1 January 2035, when Diana believes the cohort phase ended (0.6)
facts.parties: The Russian state and at least two Western states, through agencies, military research establishments and private contractors
facts.consequences: About forty thousand survivors held as a test cohort, with the flood as the delivery system

Interlude III: Major Budanov, Aleja Szucha

DATA.name: The stages of compliance
DATA.summary: The occupiers' scale for assessing how far a person has been pacified.
DATA.entry: The occupiers assess residents on a numbered scale. Stage 3 is the point at which a person will give up a name when asked. Stage 4 is the point at which they will give up one without being asked. Stage 5 is reported to the operator at R0 as not his concern. The district dashboard shows a cohort status, a percentage of the district assessed at Stage 3 or above, which stood at 71.2 per cent on the day recorded. The rota sends crews to collect persons assessed at Stage 4 who are non-ambulant. At the Poniatowski Bridge checkpoint, arrivals are assessed on the bridge at Stage 2 or 3 and passed to a reception hall. The scale is not the same as the medical staging of pressure sores, which one carer also records as Stage 2 and then Stage 4. Two accounts of the stages exist. Catalina Chmielewska's clinical table in Protocol 003 gives four, by time of continuous exposure, from unusual calm within four hours at stage 1 to compliance after four days at stage 4, where a person follows any instruction without hostility. The occupiers read the same stages by behaviour. In Interlude III, Budanov records that at stage 1 a subject refuses the water, at stage 2 drinks it quickly with a tremor, at stage 3 drinks it steadily and holds the glass in both hands, and at stage 4 neither drinks nor declines. A stage 0 appears in the screening records and on the dashboard in Interlude V, where a person at stage 0 is noted as resistant. The brief described in Protocol 005 names stage 4 as the target state. Protocol 005 also uses the word stage for the three phases of the destruction of Żerań, which is unrelated.
DATA.appears: Chapter 9: The Dendron (Protocol 003), section 5. Chapter 7: The Musician, Diana's diary of 17 November 2034, for patients at stage 2. Interlude I: Wiktor Szeliga, Block C, for the staging of a pressure sore. Interlude II: Sasha Lebedev, Observation Post R0. Interlude III: Major Budanov, Aleja Szucha. Interlude V: Account Lead, Cohort Review. Chapter 15: The Aftermath (Protocol 005), section 7. Chapter 16: The Protocols, Diana's diary of 28 December 2034.
DATA.reliability: C (7 passages: Chapters 7, 9, 15 and 16 and Interludes II, III and V). Stages 1 to 4 are defined in Protocol 003 section 5 and, by behaviour, in Interlude III, and the two agree in order. Stage 0 appears in two passages and is defined only by the remarks on a dashboard record: E. Stage 5 is named once, in Interlude II, and is not defined: E.

facts.parties: The occupiers, who read the stages by behaviour. Catalina Chmielewska, whose clinical table gives them by exposure
facts.consequences: At stage 3 a person gives up a name when asked. Stage 4 is the target state of the programme

Interlude II: Sasha Lebedev, Observation Post R0

DATA.name: The Warsaw Uprising of 1944
DATA.summary: The historical parallel the survivors and Diana draw on.
DATA.entry: Marek Olszewski gave the following account. In 1944 the Home Army rose against the German occupation and fought for sixty-three days. It was destroyed. During those days the Red Army stood on the east bank of the Vistula, within sight of the city, and did not cross. When the rising failed, the German command razed what remained of the city, block by block, with explosives and fire, as punishment. Of the city on the left bank, eighty-five per cent was destroyed. The Old Town and Royal Castle were rebuilt afterwards from photographs and paintings. Marek also told the story of a Home Army captain in the sewers under Śródmieście in August: a hard man who held his line for three weeks because his men believed he would never leave them. In September the men found a note in his coat offering him terms. He had not accepted it, and had not burned it either. He kept it four days. Marek's judgement was that the men could not forgive that he was a good man who had kept the door open. Diana describes the destruction of Żerań in terms of 1944, and says the comparison was given to her and she declined to refuse it. Marek told Diana the account over tea, in a kitchen with the children under the table, and said he had spent ninety years waiting for someone to say it aloud. He told the story of the captain on Thursday 30 November 2034, to eleven people in his and Rosa's flat in Białołęka. Zoysa Zieliński was in the room and thanked him formally before leaving without her coat. Diana sets 1944 beside Żerań in a table of six rows and does not claim that the two are the same, only that the author of the second knew the first. Protocol 002 records the Old Town as occupied for its symbolism, with loudspeakers on the ramparts.
DATA.appears: Chapter 15: The Aftermath (Protocol 005), sections 2 and 6, the testimony of M. Olszewski and the table of the two events. Chapter 11: The Orphan, Diana's diary of 30 November 2034, for the captain in the sewers. Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), section 5.3, for the Old Town rebuilt after 1944.
DATA.reliability: C (3 passages: Chapters 15, 11 and 6). The sixty-three days, the Red Army and the eighty-five per cent rest on Marek alone, rated 0.7 as source 9 in Protocol 005. The rebuilding from photographs is stated independently in Protocol 002 section 5.3. The captain story is told once, as heard by Diana.

facts.parties: The Home Army, the German occupation, and the Red Army on the east bank
facts.consequences: The rising was destroyed after sixty-three days and 85 per cent of the left-bank city was razed. The Old Town was rebuilt from photographs and paintings

DATA.name: Street names
DATA.summary: Survivors navigate by street names that were withdrawn before 1944.
DATA.entry: Many streets in the flooded corridor are passable only under names that the municipal authority withdrew before 1944. Those are the names in use among the survivors and the ones that will be understood. A list of forty-one streets, with both names, is given in Annex A, which is held in binder two and not reproduced. The Foreword describes the Protocols as listing streets that no longer existed under names unused since 1944. The Protocol gives no individual street name, and no other passage in the manuscript gives one, so the list is not available to the reader.
DATA.appears: Foreword. Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), section 10.
DATA.reliability: C (2 passages: the Foreword and Protocol 001 section 10). Annex A is not reproduced, so none of the forty-one pairs of names can be checked.

facts.period: Withdrawn before 1944. In use in the corridor in 2034
facts.parties: The survivors, and the municipal authority that withdrew the names
facts.consequences: Many streets are passable only under the old names. Annex A lists forty-one

DATA.name: Rising water
DATA.summary: Why the flood does not recede.
DATA.entry: The water has not receded because the causes have not been corrected. Reservoirs are damaged and cannot absorb rainfall. The dam at Włocławek is non-functional. Breached dikes cannot be repaired under occupation. Pumping stations have no power. The occupiers prioritise their own routes and show no interest in civilian drainage (E). The water plateaus and does not pass. Protocol 001 gives the causes as a cascade of five failures upstream between 11 and 16 October 2028, at Solina, Czorsztyn, Sandomierz, Włocławek and the Narew retention works. It puts the corridor at 84 m, plus or minus 0.4 m with rainfall, against a pre-flood datum of 77 m, read daily at the Żerań dock gauge. The explanation is graded E, and the manuscript shows the occupiers doing more than neglect the water. Lucasz Kowalski, who wrote the gate sequence of the Vistula Canal, says that those who took the control room swapped two lines, so that the canal brings water in. The third flood, on the night of 31 December 2034, is recorded as an act. The gates were opened in sequence with the lower gates held shut, and the Żerań gauge rose from 84.3 m at 21:00 to 88.6 m at 02:05.
DATA.appears: Chapter 3: The Zone (Protocol 001), sections 2 and 3. Chapter 4: The Engineer, Lucasz Kowalski's recording of December 2035. Interlude: The Second Flood, Diana's diary of 2 September 2034. Chapter 15: The Aftermath (Protocol 005), sections 3 and 4.
DATA.reliability: E (1 passage for the explanation, which is Diana's assessment in Protocol 001 section 3). Three further passages, Chapter 4, the Second Flood interlude and Protocol 005, record the events themselves.

facts.period: From the upstream failures of 11 to 16 October 2028 to the third flood of 31 December 2034
facts.parties: The occupiers, who took the canal control room. Lucasz Kowalski, who wrote its gate sequence
facts.consequences: The corridor stands at 84 m against a pre-flood datum of 77 m, and the water does not recede

DATA.name: Screening
DATA.summary: The occupiers' seven step procedure for establishing the stage of each subject, as run by Major Budanov at Aleja Szucha.
DATA.entry: Screening is the procedure by which the occupiers establish the stage of each person brought to them. Protocol 002 names the screening camps and their head, Major Budanov, and says that what the screening consists of is not known to Diana. Interlude III gives the procedure. It is seven steps, on pages 61 to 88 of a ring-bound procedures binder of 212 pages, in Russian with a Polish translation. A committee wrote it. Budanov revised it in his first week, to take out what was unnecessary, and the word distress in its opening sentence is his. That sentence gives the purpose: to establish, in the shortest time and with the least distress, the stage of each subject. The steps are reception, observation, baseline, the offer, questions, recording and disposition. In observation the subject is watched in silence for between ninety seconds and three minutes, and the stage is read from what the subject does with a glass of water. At stage 1 the subject refuses it. At stage 2 the subject drinks it quickly, with a tremor. At stage 3 the subject drinks it steadily and holds the glass in both hands. At stage 4 the subject neither drinks nor declines. The baseline is five questions, on name, address, date of birth, occupation and nearest relations, with the delay before each answer noted in seconds. In the offer a boiled sweet is held out. About half of the subjects at stage 3 take it, and all at stage 4. The questions then ask for the names of persons hostile to the order of the district, without a raised voice or any touch. A clerk behind glass transcribes the answers in triplicate. The interviewer writes the stage and one of four decisions: Release, Retain, Transfer or Treat. The last two are not explained on any form that Alex has read. A one page annex to the binder, headed Acoustic Conditioning and unsigned, gives a low sound of about 180 hertz with a beat of six seconds, to be played beneath the table for a subject in the first days of exposure. It is not one of the seven steps, and the subject is not told of it. The screening record runs to 4,100 numbered forms, found in eleven boxes in a basement in Praga. Alex has read about three hundred. On one form the box for the sweet is blank. The subject is an interpreter, a woman of forty-one, assessed at stage 0, and the margin carries a note in Budanov's hand that she did not take it and that he is curious about her. The room, the lamp and the manner of the interviewer in the reconstruction are Alex's own and are not tagged to a source.
DATA.appears: Chapter 6: The Occupation (Protocol 002), sections 6 and 7.2, where the screening camps are named and the content of the screening is said to be unknown; Interlude III: Major Budanov, Aleja Szucha, in full
DATA.reliability: C for the seven steps, the page numbers, the four decisions and the form with the blank sweet: one passage, Interlude III, which rests on the binder and the forms as Alex reports them. E for the room and the manner of delivery, which Alex says he supplied. Protocol 002 names the camps and their head, and states that the content of screening is not known to Diana: U. Three passages in all.

facts.parties: Major Budanov and his staff at Aleja Szucha, and the persons brought in
facts.consequences: Each subject is released, retained, transferred or treated. The record runs to 4,100 forms
